speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a question of privilege because I believe it is the privilege of every member to obtain as accurate a reply as possible when information is sought from a department and the officials of such department are required to give a reply.
Question No. 2,721, which I put on the order paper some time ago about Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation followed a question asked a few weeks previously to find out who were the notaries writing the contracts for the purchase of houses in Lebel-sur-Quevillon in the riding of Chapleau. The answer at that time was that the services of notary Real
Inquiries o] the Ministry Caron of Senneterre and notary Joseph Morin of Val d'Or were being used. I was asking for additional information and I was refused for instance data on the amounts paid to each of these notaries while given to understand that both wrote notarized contracts.
To question No. 2,721, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), replied that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had approved 335 loans for an amount of nearly $5.8 million in Lebel-sur-Quevillon for 378 units of housing. Of these, 92 loans have been cancelled, and 243 are active loans for 286 units.
To the direct question: How many of these loans required the services of Mr. Real Caron of Senneterre, the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation replied: none. Yet, two or three weeks previously, I was told that notary Caron of Senneterre had drawn up contracts for houses at Lebel-sur-Quevillon.
To the third part of the question:
How many of these loans have required the services of Mr. Joseph Morin?
The answer was 243; that is the total number of the loans.
Mr. Speaker, the reason is not given why the services of notary Caron were not used. I should like to observe here after securing the information, that notary Morin-and I do not want to play politics-was the Liberal candidate in my riding at the last election and these contracts bring him $250 each which amounts to $70,750.
So, Mr. Speaker, I believe my question of privilege is quite in order and I should ask the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation before the house to state clearly whether this corporation has been established for political patronage or to give justice to the citizens of Canada wherever they may be.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we on this side advocated all along that the unification bill should have been sent to the defence committee before second reading or approval in principle. I wonder how many hon. members, particularly on the other side of the chamber, would have voted for second reading if they had heard the evidence given in
April 10, 1967	COMMONS
the defence committee. Speaking of the evidence given in the defence committee, I quote from a publication of the Tri-Service Identities Organization:
It is noteworthy that not one recently retired senior officer no longer having any attachment to the department of defence has supported the program which will be carried forward if Bill C-243 is enacted and everyone of any stature outside the services or government whose military opinion would command respect who has testified before the defence committee has expressed criticism or reservation on the proposed reorganization of the defence establishment.
I wonder, particularly, how many hon. members opposite have carefully read the evidence given by Air Chief Marshal Miller. In referring to Air Chief Marshal Miller I quote from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 22. The editorial is headed "An Unseemly Rush To What?" It reads as follows:
When Air Chief Marshal Frank Miller retired last July, he did so quietly, without any comment about differences over unification then roiling the armed forces. Until that point, as the first chief of the integrated defence staff, he had been defence minister Paul Hellyer's right hand man-how significantly so is indicated by the fact that he had been persuaded to stay three years past the normal retirement age of 55.
The testimony which Air Chief Marshal Miller gave to the Commons defence committee this week is, therefore, of peculiar importance, for it is the testimony of a man who had the regard of the minister, who personified integration, and who studiously observed the duty of an officer not to comment publicly on matters of public policy.
I will not quote at length from Air Chief Marshal Miller's testimony but merely give his reply to just one question. I quote from the Gazette of Saturday, April 8:
Air Marshal, you have indicated in answer to Mr. Harkness that you saw no advantages to unification. Did I understand you correctly when you said you could list several disadvantages?
Here is the answer:
I said I did not see any monetary return for unification, nor did I see any significant military effectiveness. I said I saw some unanswered questions associated with unification that perhaps should be spelled out before you could really get out and attempt to sell it to people-Gentlemen, could I say thank you for your courtesy and understanding.
And so on. Then Air Chief Marshal Miller said:
I feel the next step that was forecast in the white paper, that of doing away with the services, will cause the loss, against this business we have been discussing recently, of a lot of people we cannot afford to lose and that we will not get very much of a benefit from this single service proposal.
I wonder how hon. members opposite would have voted in favour on second reading had
National Defence Act Amendment they had that advice from Air Chief Marshal Miller. I wonder, for example, how the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) feels after having read the evidence of Air Chief Marshal Miller.
I know that the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) was not there at that time-incidentally we are all very happy that he has been able to return to the chamber-but I am sure that he has since read the evidence of Air Chief Marshal Miller and I hope that he has not changed the position he took last October. I should like to quote the following from a letter he wrote dated October 20, 1966:
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
On the subject of unification, I understand your views and my position at the moment is that I am awaiting the introduction of the government's legislation on unification. Complete unification is of course not practical, nor is it contemplated. The degree of unification the government proposes will very largely influence my own position.
Yours sincerely,
David W. Groos,
M.P. for Victoria, B.C.
The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) made a speech on unification in the house on January 31. However, all he said on the subject matter of the bill was the following, as found on page 12468 of Hansard:
I have purposely refrained, Mr. Speaker, from entering into the subject of the debate because, as chairman of the defence committee, I feel it is my most important duty, if this bill ever does come before us, to help resolve the differences during the clause by clause study in committee.
The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) is no longer chairman of the defence committee but it is my belief that, based on his distinguished record in the Royal Canadian Navy, he will be anxious to let his true thoughts on unification be known, and we look forward to his speech in the near future. I know that his constituents are anxiously waiting to hear from him. I myself was not able to become a member of the defence committee. I asked to be placed on the committee but that was not possible, and since I was a member of five other committees it was not possible for me to attend many of the meetings. However, I believe I read all the evidence given before the defence committee.
It is true that mostly as a result of the form of questioning of witnesses some of the evidence was conflicting. But that does not justify hon. members on the other side, who are no doubt making speeches for consumption in their home ridings, taking quotations completely out of context so that the people reading their speeches may be led to believe that a
14710	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment certain person who gave evidence before the committee was in favour of unification even though that was not necessarily so. For example, I will quote part of the speech made by the hon. member for Hamilton West on April 5 as it appears at page 14577 of Hansard. The hon. member quotes General Foulkes as follows:
The problem can only be solved by complete unification of the three services with one chief of staff, one chain of command, one ladder of promotion and one uniform.
This is the only part of General Foulkes' evidence which the hon. member quoted. The obvious intention is to lead readers of his speech to believe that General Foulkes is completely in favour of unification. That quotation was taken from an article written by General Foulkes in 1961. If the hon. member had wanted to be fair he might well have quoted from a subsequent article by General Foulkes which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, October 13, 1966, in which he wrote the following:
One of the aspects of integration, which is relatively unimportant but which is causing some resentment in the services, is the announced intention to force the servicemen into a neutral uniform by 1967. Perhaps this is to be part of the "centennial" celebrations to show that Canada still maintains what a pundit once referred to as "the best dressed, best fed, best paid, but poorest equipped force in the west."
Again I quote from this article by General Foulkes:
Since any acceptable integration scheme calls for the continuation of regiments of soldiers, squadrons of aircraft and flotillas of ships, the servicemen in these combat formations must continue to wear the appropriate combat uniform.
Again I quote from the article:
We should not be mesmerized by the idea that a common uniform will ensure a happy, contented and efficient integrated service.
I quote further from the article:
The minister has not been forthright in informing the services and the public of the true and real extent of the integration plot.
Continuing on the same lines the hon. member for Hamilton West quoted General Moncel as saying the following:
I was well aware of the fact that the white paper said that unification was the ultimate end. Well, that was fine. There was nothing wrong with it as a name.
If read out of context that quotation certainly gives the impression that General Moncel was in complete agreement with the minister's plans.

An effort has been made by the minister, by some of his officials and by informed persons in his department who write the press releases to give the impression that this wonderful scheme of the unification of our armed forces is being studied carefully and might be followed by other countries. The letter from which I am quoting is dated March 14 and was written by Commodore Harold V. W. Groos, R.C.N., retired. It reads in part as follows:
Probably the last thing you would choose to become involved in is Canadian politics, yet you are now in them deeply.
Yesterday, Monday, 13th March, 1967, our last chief of the naval staff of Canada, Vice Admiral Herbert S. Rayner appeared before the Canadian House of Commons defence committee to advocate the continuance of a navy in a distinctive uniform and with a titular head to speak for it and to set standards of seagoing fighting efficiency. Under cross-examination by Liberal party politicos who are out to submerge (i.e. destroy) the Royal Canadian Navy as an ^identifiable sea force, Admiral Rayner quoted you as being in favour of retaining navies with titular heads.
Last night the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's national news summary referred to Admiral Rayner's testimony and then there was a two or three minute presentation of an interview with you which had been held at government house, Ottawa, last autumn. In your interview you supported strongly both integration and the unification of our armed forces.
Undoubtedly the television camera interview with you had been held in reserve by the Liberal politicians to discredit Admiral Rayner and in this it has succeeded admirably.
I have before me the original of the letter sent by Mountbatten of Burma, dated March 28, 1967 and commencing, "My Dear Groos". I should like to quote one paragraph from the letter:
You are quite right in saying that the last thing I would choose to become involved in is Canadian politics and I am indeed sorry that use has been made of the views I expressed during two visits to Canada which appear to involve me.
Then Lord Mountbatten encloses a statement which explains his position and I quote from this statement, of which I have the original signed by Mountbatten of Burma:
I have been asked for an explanation of my views on the integration and unification of the British services as they are said to have been misunderstood in Canada.
Then I skip part of the statement and quote this pertinent passage:
In the British reorganization care has been taken to preserve esprit de corps and morale and those traditions which help to maintain this in the services and fighting units. It has been accepted that to achieve this the three services must retain their uniforms and ranks with an identifiable professional head of their service. The idea of a single uniform and rank structure was also rejected as undesirable and unnecessary.
There was some talk of taking the uniform and ranks of one service and imposing this on the others but the idea of a man in say army uniform with an army title arriving at a foreign port in command of a warship was generally felt to be so ludicrous that it was not pursued. The general cut and colour of naval uniforms are internationally so well known
National Defence Act Amendment that a sailor from any one country can readily be recognized as a sailor in any other country. Sailors the world over take great pride in this and so in their own services do soldiers and airmen. No compensating advantage could be seen in attempting to impose so unpopular a change.
The last paragraph of Lord Mountbatten's statement, dated March 28, 1967, reads:
These were the views X expressed or intended to convey when I was asked to explain them to the Canadian press, radio and television. Nothing has happened to change these views.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I turn to the subject of the bill I want to say a few things about the standing committee on national defence which I had the honour to chair through the latter half of its sittings. It was like being a spectator at that famous Arctic poker game that Robert W. Service told us about at which all the men around the table simultaneously drew their revolvers on each other. Unlike that story, however, the committee members did not stay in that pose until they all froze to death. They held a total of 55 meetings between February 7 and March 21. They examined 28 principal witnesses and published 2,000 pages of briefs and verbal evidence. They examined and passed the 65 clauses of the bill and its lengthy schedules. Moreover, they wound up their work in time for everyone in this chamber to go home for a well deserved Easter holiday. None of the members of the committee missed more than a meeting or two and I am sure only then because of real necessity. We always had a full quorum and we had no problems getting started although as chairman I frequently had problems in getting people stopped. What we proved by our actions in that committee was that you can unify anything.
I want to say a word about the services of the committee. We were never without the services of an interpreter throughout all our hearings. We had the unfailing services of Mr. Hugh Stewart, the clerk of the committee. Despite competition from several other hard working committees, the committee reporting branch produced 5,000 folios of evidence during the hearings. All of this evidence was edited by the committees branch and then sent to the printer. Then the printing staff worked overtime through Easter to see that we received it back in time for the commencement of the committee stage of the bill in the house. Moreover, all the evidence was translated into French and the whole thing printed in French and English in time for us to use it in the house after we returned from Easter holidays.
Finally, Dr. Ollivier and the Judge Advocate General's staff incorporated all the amendments into the bill, saw that the French and English matched and produced a newly printed version for the house in time for our use. We do not often say things about the
National Defence Act Amendment servants of the house and how they serve us and I thought, Mr. Chairman, you would like to be made aware of these things at the outset of the few remarks I wish to make on the subject of the bill.
A few years ago Professor Northcote Parkinson became famous as the author of a satirical book called "Parkinson's Law". He observed that while the number of British warships had decreased by 67 per cent between 1914 and 1928, the number of admiralty officials had increased by 78 per cent. The officials, he said, would have multiplied at the same rate had there been no actual seamen at all. The fact is, he told his readers, that the number of the officials and the quantity of the work are not related to each other.
In case anyone felt that he had chosen an isolated incident on which to base his theory he noted that the colonial office, in the period of British colonial decline from 1935 to 1954, had increased its staff from 372 to 1,661.
Speaking at the University of Alberta in 1963 in the Henry Marshall Tory lecture series, Professor Parkinson threw in a couple of extra observations on his theory. He said that a correspondent had pointed out to him that an organization which has a headquarters staff of a thousand can be regarded as administratively self-sufficient. It can keep itself entirely busy on its own internal problems. Then he spoke of a certain German industrial group that apparently had a headquarters staff of 2,000 persons. All its factories were destroyed by enemy action during the war but the administrative staff went on working as hard as ever though there was nothing to administer. I mention this because Bill C-243 deals with reorganizing a big headquarters staff, big enough to be entirely self-sufficient according to Professor Parkinsons' terms.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Before we become too dazzled by military science, let me make a few observations in the Parkinsonian manner about some of the things witnesses brought up before the defence committee. In the past there have been numerous examples of integration, some workable and some not. Always these integrations took place in the field at the command level, never at headquarters. Not until the present minister came along had anybody attempted to integrate the headquarters.
If you turn to the evidence of General Foulkes you will find very interesting reminiscences of integration attempts stretching back to the time when Hon. Brooke Claxton
14714	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment was minister of national defence. He brought together the three defence ministries of wartime days. He started the idea of unifying all three services but gave it up. He set up studies and committee work in connection with integration, studies which were later pursued and developed by some of the very men who appeared before the defence committee as competent officer witnesses. General Foulkes told us in an amusing way about efforts to unify the chaplain services. During the tenure of office of Mr. Pearkes as minister of national defence the matter had ended with the addition of a brigadier to the chaplain services but with no apparent amalgamation of services.
No one will say very much if the forces are integrated at that level. I am speaking of naval or air force units, for example. The local air force commander may not want to be put under the authority of the local naval commander but he will tolerate it and the system will work after a fashion because each commander believes that the arrangement is not permanent and that he will not have to put up with the other fellow forever. The air force commander may even take comfort in dreaming that he may one day be in charge of the integrated command. That is why the minister and other ministers have been able to get along with the business of reorganizing at the command level without causing significant political flurries.
When the minister integrated his headquarters a number of things began to happen that could not happen with integration at the command levels. First, the chiefs of the three services found themselves without jobs. They had gone from the organizational structure. At the same time the three services found themselves without chiefs above the level of the command structure. There was now a new chief who represented a consolidation of the three services. The new chief of staff now stood alone at the top of the structure and had to turn his back on the old three-service organization that he had known and grown up with. He had become the chief of the new integrated commands. All this happened when Bill C-90 was passed in July, 1964. This is what Bill C-90 did. All the important operative legislative and organizational steps which we have been discussing and which were necessary to create a unified force were taken when we passed Bill C-90 in July, 1964. Let me check this out with hon. members again.

DEBATES	April 10, 1967
First, the old chiefs of the three services were retired. Second, a single chief was established in their place. Third, the officers and men of the three old services were reorganized into new functional commands or components. As I say, this is what we did through Bill C-90. Only one thing of any real importance remained to be done and that was to give the new single force which we had created in 1964 a name. Bill C-243 asks us to do that. No clause in Bill C-243, other than clause 2 before the committee now, is of any real significance. I say that because clause 2 gives the force a new name.
The clause concerning the ranks of officers has been thoroughly amended. I invite hon. members of the committee to read clause 4 and note how it has been amended and what it means now. The power to regulate how officers shall be referred to has been withdrawn from the minister and placed in the hands of cabinet. It is only possible through an order in council now to change the designations of officers or the titles by which they shall be called. By no stretch of the imagination will the bill give landlubbers' titles to seagoing men. This was one of the major complaints made, and one of the complaints raised by my hon. friend from Esquimalt-Saanich a few moments ago. He has not studied the bill. He does not know what is in it. He has not read the testimony of General Allard. He has not looked at the evidence given again and again by the minister. Yet he stands up and says the same thing that has been said many times before though the committee diligently went about its business of attending to the very point complained about.

Well, the hon. member's remark will be recorded for posterity. Members of the armed forces may find themselves with greater scope as a result of unification because they will be able to move freely across the whole width of the force. Young officers of competence will find broader opportunities available to them. The names of the units, as I have said, will not be changed. The customs and traditions of the units will not change.
One of the hon. members opposite, the hon. member for Vegreville, went to considerable pains in the committee one day to examine General Allard on this point. He did an excellent job of drawing from the general recognition of the fact that the traditions and customs of the regiments would remain and that there was no danger that these things would be taken away. I am sure he was well satisfied with the situation. Indeed, I am sure the general satisfied everyone present. Yet we still find people saying that these regiments and their traditions will be destroyed. This is nonsense, and members opposite such as the hon. member for Vegreville who have taken the trouble to find out the facts know very well that this is the case. Nevertheless the opposition has perpetuated this sham, believing that somehow or other it will have its effect upon the Canadian people who will eventually accept it as the truth. I do not believe this will ever happen.
The most radical thing which will happen to the man in the Canadian armed forces after the passage of this bill is that in due course he will get a new suit. I want to remind hon. members who have spent a considerable amount of time discussing this point that it does not require Bill C-243 in order to make that possible. The bill before us does not effect the cost of operating the forces. This was taken care of by Bill C-90. The savings to be made will result from the changes in materiel command and training command as those changes evolve. All this was provided for in Bill C-90 which was passed back in July of 1964.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are asking that we pause, that we kick this issue around like Chicago's garbage until we lose it. We do not intend to do this. The bill before us does not affect the composition of the forces. The composition of the forces was affected by Bill C-90 and those changes have now been made.

This bill has nothing to do with morale. The morale of some of those serving in the ranks reflected for a time the very low morale of their senior officers. Those were the men who got out because they did not believe that a minister should have the right to reorganize a headquarters. That is what this debate is about, basically. The Tories do not believe that a minister of the crown should have the right to reorganize a headquarters, only to tinker with the structure underneath. These are not the facts of political life. Great changes of this kind must be made at the political level. Hon. members opposite cannot evade this issue.
Finally, let me say a word to all those who say we should pause. It is necessary now to create an organization with a headquarters under a single chief responsible for functional commands working in the field. He is struggling to project a new spirit into this new organization, to teach the men new loyalities and a new esprit de corps. It is not an easy task and we do him no service by prolonging argument here for the retention of a military system which we voted out in this house when we passed Bill C-90 in July, 1964. We have said everything that can possibly be said about this matter ten times over, Mr. Chairman. It is time we stopped procrastinating. It is time to pass this bill and to give this force a new and honourable name and not leave it as a nameless child on the doorstep, something which hon. gentlemen opposite would like to do.

Mr. Chairman, during the past week we witnessed strange happenings on the other side of the chamber with Liberal members, one after the other, standing up and reading from prepared texts contrary to what the rules provide. I wonder whether they were reading for the very simple reason that they have joined the minister's propaganda team and are not allowed to express one thought of their own lest they might say something not in agreement with the minister's propaganda.
The other day the hon. member for Lamb-ton West speaking or, I should say, reading his prepared text made reference to my attitude while serving on the defence committee and said that when the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona and myself joined the committee it became partisan and we began insulting serving officers. At that time I asked him how many serving officers appeared before the committee while I served on it and he said he did not know. I draw his attention, the attention of the minister and that of every Grit opposite to the fact that I was not on the defence committee for the complete examination of one serving officer. This, Mr. Chairman, will give you an idea of the approach of the Liberal party when we have one of its members standing up and accusing me of something which I could not possibly have done. Furthermore, the implication that the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona and I joined the committee at the same time is entirely wrong.
Despite what the Minister of National Defence may think I wish to tell him that he does not have the support for his unification bill within his own party that he would like to have. Some of its members have different opinions from his and that is why each and every Grit who stands up has had to read word for word from a prepared text, with one exception. The exception was the Minister of Transport who became exercised on Friday afternoon, jumped into the debate without the permission of the Minister of National Defence and, without notes, put his foot in it. I
National Defence Act Amendment shall refer to what he said later, but he was the one exception and it was a mistake on their part to allow him to speak because he got excited.
Even the Secretary of State for External Affairs read word for word from a prepared text. Granted, he was dealing with foreign policy rather than with the unification bill. The minister is shaking his head. Before I am finished he will have a lot of shaking to do.
Since the hon. member for Lambton West saw fit to criticize me perhaps the best thing I could do would be to review the committee hearings to see what his attitude was. But I will have to forego that. He did not have an attitude in the defence committee so I cannot criticize something that was non-existent. The hon. member referred to the membership of the committee. How can the Liberal members who participated in the defence committee have followed what went on? Reference was made to the fact that I and other members in this party were involved in changes in the membership of the committee. For every Conservative change in membership on the defence committee there were at least six Liberal changes, a total of 41 changes on that side of the chamber. How could they have kept up with the evidence? They were shuffling in and out day after day. Not one of them liked to spend too much time on the committee.
We have just heard from the man who said he had the honour to lead the defence committee in the last half of its sessions. I repeat he said he had the honour to lead it. All I can say is that it is too bad he could not have turned that around and led the committee with honour. He did not lead with honour because on March 3 in this house, the first day he participated in the committee, he came into the house and made a report from the committee which was far removed from the truth, and the House of Commons spent the greatest part of the afternoon on a question of privilege in reference to his action as defence committee chairman.

I would then call the minister's attention to the March 3 committee hearings, page 1960, where he will see for himself a complete denial of what was said by the chairman of the defence committee in the house. The chairman of the defence committee came into the House of Commons and reported something that had never happened. It is

This is another indication that hon. members on that side of the chamber are still trying to push something down our throats despite the fact-and I refer to what the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona brought out very clearly-that serving officers could only give evidence to the defence committee based on government policy and could not

[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I should like to go back to the Minister of Transport. The Minister of National Defence will realize that the Minister of Transport jumped in because he was excited. He jumped in even though he did not have the benefit of the propaganda which has been available to the Minister of National Defence. He still made some strange statements. When I asked him whether he would permit a question, in his usual rude way he refused to give me that opportunity. Mr. Chairman, you and I know that over the years the matter of courtesy and rudeness between the Minister of Transport and I has been a debatable issue. So far rudeness and courtesy between the Minister of Transport and I are concerned, I believe we are almost even. He is away ahead on rudeness and I am ahead on courtesy.
I do not have the words of the Minister of Transport in front of me but at one point when he was trying to justify a unified force he said that there never has been a unified force. I do not know whether the minister realized it, but he was contradicting many members on the Liberal side of the house. Liberal members have held up the United States marines as an example of a unified force, which it is not, and in general have stated that it was the government's idea to pattern its force on the United States Marines. This statement has been made by members of the Liberal party and contradicts the statement made by the Minister of Transport.
Hon. members will remember also a rather strange statement made by the Minister of Transport not too long ago. He turned to the Prime Minister at a time when Conservative and other opposition members were accusing the government of backpeddling and retreating and said to his own Prime Minister that as usual he would have to backtrack. This was a very amazing statement. I did not think it could be improved upon until the minister spoke in the house on Friday. On Friday the minister made a statement which I think should be given some attention. As found on page 14668 of Hansard, the last paragraph, the minister is reported as having said:
If the minister accepts the wrong advice and adopts the wrong course, of course he should be defeated.
April 10, 1967

I will be much more generous and say that if he should not be defeated he should at least resign his portfolio. The former minister of finance resigned his position because he had given the Prime Minister the wrong advice. According to the Minister of Transport, we should have the resignation of the Minister of National Defence.
I should like to turn now to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who in support of the Minister of National Defence last week made a few strange statements. He read his speech and spoke entirely on foreign affairs. In answer to a question concerning a statement made by General Allard and later published, the Minister of National Defence stood up in the house and said that he had confidence in General Allard and that General Allard did not have to clear his statements with him. Apparently the Minister of National Defence does not know the rules. Not only does the minister have to clear such speeches but he also has to give permission for them to be made.
This matter was brought up earlier by the hon. member for Kootenay West. At that time he asked a question in respect of a German who was to speak before a group in Winnipeg. The answer given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was that he had no intention to interfere with freedom of speech. Last week the Minister of National Defence implied that General Allard can go wherever he wishes and say whatever he likes. The minister was entirely wrong and the Secretary of State for External Affairs was also wrong when he answered the hon. member for Kootenay West. The German in question was not allowed to speak in Winnipeg, or at least did not speak. The Minister of National Defence not only has erred but in addition he has received incorrect advice as is evident by the mistake made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of National Defence to the Queen's Rules and Regulations. The latest edition available to me is one I obtained from the Parliamentary Library. I should like to refer this to the minister as recommended reading. He should know at least the basic rules which apply to serving personnel in this country. Paragraph 679 reads as follows:
The publication or disclosure of any form of unpublished official documents, or of their contents, or of official information to unauthorized persons, or the use of such documents or information in personal controversy or for any private purpose, without due sanction from superior military authority, is forbidden.
National Defence Act Amendment
The paragraph 680 (a) contains the following:
An officer or soldier is forbidden to publish in any form whatever, or communicate, either directly or indirectly, to the press, any military information, or his views on any military subject, without War Office authority. He is further forbidden without first obtaining War Office permission, to deliver any lecture or discourse, or to answer questions, on any military subject, either publicly or by means of broadcasting or television, or to prepare a paper or write a script on any military subject for delivery or transmission to the public. He will not prejudge questions which are under the consideration of superior military authority by the publication, anonymously or otherwise, of his opinions, and he will not take part, in public, in a discussion relating to orders, regulations or instructions issued by his superiors.
There it is in black and white. The Minister of National Defence does not know the simple rules which apply to serving officers. This brings us back to the fact that the ultimate authority over the military in this country is a civilian one. It is about time the minister re-examined his position and looked carefully down the road he is leading the forces of this country. The evidence contradicts what has been said by the Minister of National Defence in the house and supports the statements made by other members of the government in respect of certain adverse remarks which have been made. As I have pointed out, the Secretary of State for External Affairs found himself out in left field in respect of questions pertaining to freedom of speech when military matters are involved.

The Minister of National Defence apparently thinks he has the support of his members and believes that unification is a good thing. I come back to what I have stated before in the house on the question of unification. Canada has always been proud of the fact that we have had volunteer forces. In the committee the Liberal members voted against the opportunity to re-attest being given to every serving man in our forces. In other words, as I said before, what they have been doing is voting for conscription. It is nothing more nor less than conscription because every man serving in the forces today will be serving under compulsion unless he is given the opportunity to re-attest. It will no longer be a volunteer force.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief remarks on this important bill but I must say at the outset that I am not an expert on military matters; in fact my military experience is very limited. I was a member of the Church Lads Brigade. I have been a boy scout and a scoutmaster. I have been a member of the Arrow Lakes Rifles affiliated with the Rocky Mountain Rangers, and I served with the 54th Kootenay Battalion in the first world war. Later I graduated from the School of Guards which was operated in France during the first world war by the Brigade of Guards. Therefore you see, Mr. Chairman, that I am not really knowledgeable enough with respect to military strategy and tactics even to write a book.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me a question? The hon. member is pretending he did not see active service overseas although I believe he did. Was the hon. member not wounded at the Somme? Was he not in the trenches serving with the other members of the Canadian forces at that time and was he not honourably discharged after having performed his duty to his country?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply I will give the same answer I gave to the old lady who visited me in hospital in London. I told her I was bitten by a German wasp on five occasions.
I said that I do not profess to have sufficient knowledge of military strategy and tactics even to write a book. All I have done in this respect was to write a script for the local

dramatic society which dealt with the well-known Bairnsfather character, Old Bill, and Colonel Blimp. That was the only production in the literary sense with which I have had anything to do. So I trust all hon. members will realize that I am speaking as an amateur on this subject and from a somewhat different point of view to that of my hon. friends to my right.
However, I do want to say that I know people feel very deeply on this question. They have strong feelings on both sides of the question and they express themselves very vehemently on occasions. I must say I do not like personal remarks in a debate of this kind. I think we can take a dig or two and make certain cogent references now and again as long as we retain our sense of humour, but if we are to maintain a certain standard we must present our views, in regard to policy as if we were gentlemen. I remember that my mother always said a gentleman was a man who always acted properly and never did anything wrong in public. I wish that members of this house would take my mother's advice in that respect.
The attitude of the New Democratic Party to the unification of the armed forces is based on our policy with respect to foreign affairs, the United Nations, and our defence policy with respect to NATO, NORAD and nuclear weapons. So there will be no mistake with respect to our policy I wish to place on the record the resolution adopted by the New Democratic Party at one of its national conventions. I wish to refer to the program which was adopted at our convention of August, 1963 held in Regina. Of course this program has been carried forward to this date. I wish to emphasize the rather different approach we have to this problem from that of hon. members on my right. Let me say before I go any further that I do not think any of us has any objection to integration but there are different and varying reasons for opposing what is termed unification. I should like to quote the resolution which reads as follows:
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
NATO has played its part in the maintenance of west European security. However, it has concentrated on a military role and has failed to adapt its policies to the growing importance of the economic and social front in the present world struggle. The New Democratic Party believes that we should seek a reappraisal and change of NATO's policies and objectives.
The New Democratic Party believes that the extension of nuclear weapons to any further states and alliances threatens disaster to the world. It therefore opposes Canada's troops being supplied with such weapons at home or abroad.
April 10, 1967	COMMONS
At present, except for those nations which have independently developed atomic capacity, neither NATO itself nor its members individually possess or control nuclear warheads. Should they do so, Canada must make it clear that it cannot remain in the alliance. To relieve tensions, Canada should press for a demilitarized zone in central Europe and for the simultaneous disbandment of the Warsaw and NATO pacts.
I must remind the house that in reply to a question of mine addressed to the Minister of National Defence some time last year he said that NATO was a nuclear alliance. Therefore, according to our national convention resolution we propose that Canada should withdraw her forces from the alliance. This was the basis upon which this resolution was supported by our convention.
I go now to our attitude to NORAD. In this respect I wish to quote from page 51 of the New Democratic Party program. I want to be exact in this respect because possibly some members actually do not understand our resolutions.
It is questionable whether NORAD ever made any significant contribution to the defence of Canada, and in any case it has outlived its usefulness.
Furthermore, there is every danger that the Bomarcs will be equipped with nuclear warheads. The NORAD agreements should therefore be terminated.
That is the attitude of the New Democratic Party with respect to NORAD.
I might say I had a most interesting experience when I visited NORAD, and I think the minister got some of the backwash from it. We were there for three days and were lectured by the United States officers in charge of these installations. They treated us very well indeed. Just as we were leaving the gentleman in charge said to one of the members, what is your politics, sir? He said, I am a Liberal. The same question was asked of the next member and he said, I am a Conservative. The next member said he was a member of the Social Credit party, and when asked I said I was a revolutionary socialist. When we returned to Ottawa people had heard all about this and wanted to know what I had been up to. I had really made this comment in a sort of a humorous vein but it was taken seriously and resulted in an inquiry about me so far as security was concerned.

speechtext: Was your own party upset when you said this?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
No, I would not do anything of that sort, you know. We stand united except when we are apart.
Our policy with respect to NATO and NORAD is supported by other groups in Canada,
National Defence Act Amendment including the Voice of Women, and in that connection I wish to quote a statement issued by that organization:
Following the publication of the white paper on defence, Voice of Women notes that the government recognizes that Canada's defence policy cannot be dissociated from her foreign policy.
Voice of Women acknowledges the usefulness and efficiency of the integration of the armed forces but notes with concern contradictions and discrepancies between the declaration of Canada and her representatives at the United Nations and Geneva and the contents of the white paper.
I am going to give a few examples because I have a lot of correspondence with various ladies in the Voice of Women and all my life I have taken a great deal of pleasure in pleasing the ladies.
The question of nuclear weapons for the Canadian armed forces is subordinate to that of Canada's political possibility as a member of a nuclear armed alliance.
When Canada joined NATO in 1949 NATO was not a nuclear alliance. When NATO became a nuclear alliance in December, 1957, Canada could not withdraw in view of article 13 of the North Atlantic treaty which prevents withdrawal before 1969. On the other hand, it is a fact that some countries, members of NATO, have refused all nuclear weapons while remaining in the alliance.
According to the white paper, the first objective in time and in importance of Canadian defence policy is collective measures for maintenance of peace and security as embodied in the charter of the United Nations, including the search for balanced and controlled disarmament. I am very pleased to note the discussions that have been taking place in recent months at Geneva in this respect.
On January 5, 1964, the Prime Minister said that he believes Canada's future military role will require a diminution of nuclear arms and equipment. How, therefore, can the white paper recommend nuclear arms for a nuclear role for Canada's armed forces? This is a question asked by the ladies in the Voice of Women.
The white paper states that the alliance must continue to possess nuclear weapons in the absence of controlled disarmament. The greatest obstacle to controlled disarmament at the present time is precisely the possession by NATO of nuclear weapons in ever-increasing quantities.
Our position with respect to NATO is being supported by an increasing number of people with some knowledge of the circumstances. For instance, recently Hon. Howard Green,
April 10, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment former secretary of state for external affairs, was quoted in the Vancouver Province as saying that Canada should consider dropping out of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization when the present treaty expires in 1969. I might say that Mr. Green was in the same company as me for several years. I always had high regard for him. He is not a person to make a statement just to catch the press. He is a most serious-minded person and I knew him as such in civilian life, in the army and while he was secretary of state for external affairs.
The present Leader of the Opposition was quoted in an article in the Nelson Daily News of December 18, 1966, entitled "Diefenbaker Urges Cut In Canada's Force In Europe", as follows:
Opposition Leader Diefenbaker has added his voice to the growing chorus seeking a Canadian troop reduction in Europe.
I may that we in this party are very pleased indeed that the Leader of the Opposition is commencing to march in our direction. This is not the only case in which he has commenced to march in our direction. He has done so on several other occasions in recent months. Numerous editors across Canada are also beginning to realize that the defence policy of Canada must be altered to meet changing circumstances. It is for this reason the hon. member for Vancouver East said, when speaking in the house on January 30 last:
Canada should think not just of renegotiating its position in NATO but of getting out of NATO.
Later in the same speech he said:
No reasonable explanation can be given why, in regard to defence co-operation and our relations with the United States under NORAD, we should have nuclear weapons in the hands of Canadians and on Canadian soil.
Later he went on to say:
The policy of integration seems logical and reasonable to us, but the House of Commons should not be asked to endorse the principle of unification until the government has clearly outlined its attitude to existing military alliances and its reasons for the same, and the anticipated role for Canada's armed forces.
Later the same day the hon. member for Greenwood supported this point of view in similarly vigorous language. After this bill received second reading it was referred to the committee on national defence. A good many witnesses were heard both for and against the bill. I have not had the opportunity of reading all the evidence carefully, but I have picked out the evidence of those persons who received particular attention in the press or whose evidence was discussed by members in

conversation. I was particularly impressed by the evidence given by General Moncel and by Air Chief Marshal Miller, who was Canada's chief of defence staff until his early retirement last summer. I was particularly impressed with some of the questions put to him in the committee and I should like to quote one. This is a man of authority and knowledge, and he was asked this question:
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Air Marshal, you have indicated in answer to Mr. Harkness that you saw no advantages to unification. Did I understand you correctly when you said you could list several disadvantages?
Air Chief Marshal Miller replied:
I said I did not see any monetary return for unification-
Which in effect means no savings.
-nor did I see any significant military effectiveness.
When dealing with this type of legislation I think we have to pay particular attention to the opinions of one who so recently was Canada's chief of defence staff.
Passing from the evidence brought before the committee, I was interested to note an editorial in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, March 25, entitled "Where Are We Going". The article commenced:
Two New Democratic members of parliament, Andrew Brewin and Harold Winch, have at last put the dispute over unification of the armed forces in its proper context. Unification makes sense, they pointed out in a statement after the defence committee reported the bill back to the Commons, only-
The word "only" is the key word, Mr. Chairman.
-if the government intends to make drastic alterations in its present NATO and NORAD commitments. They would not, they indicated, support final passage of the bill until the government agreed to these alterations.
That is pretty definite.
Had NATO developed into some form of economic community, as once foreseen by Louis St. Laurent and Lester Pearson, there might be reasons for maintaining our part in it. It did not. We should bring our forces home. We can fulfil any responsibility to our European allies through treaties that could, for example, commit forces to their assistance in time of need.
There is also another purpose served by our armed forces: the preservation of peace in Canada itself. However much as we resent the thought, it has been necessary at times for them to play that role, and could be again.
Beyond all of this, of course, is the peacekeeping role, at which Canadians have distinguished themselves and which is undoubtedly, so far as most Canadians are concerned, the role we would wish our armed forces to play.
April 10, 1967

The military correspondent of the Globe and Mail is writing, I think, with considerable balance and thought in using these arguments. The editorial continues:
In fact, most Canadians are much more interested in preserving peace than preparing for war. Making larger forces available to police duties is one way of achieveing such an objective. Another is through ever-increasing amounts of foreign aid to underdeveloped nations. Abject poverty feeds international unrest. Could Canada shift its defence emphasis from the manifestations to the causes of unrest?
I thought that quotation from the editorial in the Globe and Mail was very interesting indeed.
During the present debate the hon. member for Greenwood placed some interesting information on the record with respect to the evidence given by General Moncel. Later the hon. member made these remarks, as reported at page 14447 of Hansard April 3:
In my view, Mr. Chairman, this reveals the essence of the matter which is facing the house today. General Moncel put his finger on precisely the real issue. However much it may be obscured by the discussions of unification, the real issue is that unification makes sense if the concentration is to be on a single mobile force which will be available for peacekeeping and other activities, but if the present roles are to be continued then it does not make sense.
The members of our group agree wholeheartedly with this point of view.
On April 5 the hon. member for Vancouver East made a very interesting speech in which he clearly indicated that it was the responsibility of the government to inform the House of Commons of the role of the armed forces, and that this party would have to make its decision on this bill according to what we believe is best for the armed forces and for Canada. In concluding his remarks the hon. member said, as reported at page 14573 of Hansard:
In the final analysis, we will search our consciences and vote in the way we think is right for the future of Canada.
According to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to whose speech I listened carefully the other day, Canada has no intention of getting out of either NATO or NORAD. With respect to NATO he said that Canadian forces contributed to existing stability in Europe and that unilateral withdrawal of them could have significant political consequences. In effect, he said that the role of the Canadian armed forces was to continue as at present. In saying this he failed to meet the suggestion put forward by our party when this bill was first discussed before it went to
National Defence Act Amendment the committee, as well as during the committee hearings and in the course of this debate, that the role of the armed forces should be to defend Canada and provide peace keeping forces for the United Nations when required.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, in another respect this debate has been somewhat disappointing in that it has not given the Canadian people any clear idea as to the cost of defence in the future, and I think they are entitled to know this. General Moncel, the former vice chief of the general staff, told the defence committee that Canada will require a budget of $2 billion to meet her commitments. I am informed that the associates of the minister have not confirmed or denied this statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few comments on Bill C-243, commonly known as the armed forces unification bill.
I have had the privilege of serving on the defence committee in the past but I did not serve on the committee when it considered this bill. Personally, I felt it was desirable to have personnel on the committee who have served in the armed forces of Canada, particularly as we are concerned about the defence of our country and the defence of freedom everywhere.
This parliament has many such distinguished members. On this side of the house in our party there are many such members who served with dedication and distinction during world war I and world war II. These men gained personal and practical knowledge of the structure of our armed forces, the structure of our defence philosophy and the structure of actual combat. Many of us do not have this experience. As one who did not serve in the armed forces of Canada I felt that a wise course for me to follow was to listen to the views of those with experience and practical knowledge. I also feel that a wise minister of national defence should follow a similar course.
I have followed the proceedings of the defence committee in the examination of the bill


now before us. It is disturbing to me, as I am sure it is disturbing to Canadians everywhere, to read the testimony of so many former senior officers who have come out squarely against the principle of the bill and who in fact maintain that the present bill, if passed, will destroy the effectiveness of the armed forces of Canada. These are men who have dedicated their whole lives to the service of their country in peacetime and in war. These men are not seeking glory or personal gain but are expressing their views based on many years of experience. There sole aim is that our country be provided with the best and most effective defence force possible. They have no ulterior motives nor axes to grind. They have the welfare of their country at heart. We as members of parliament also, I hope, place the welfare of our country first.
It is most disturbing to see the long list of senior officers who have taken early retirement or who have been fired for expressing views different from those of the minister or opposing the intent of the bill before us. The calibre of the men who have left the army, navy and air force is exceptionally high. With so much opposition to this bill and with so much doubt expressed about any beneficial effects from it, I would think that the minister would be wise to go slowly and to take a closer look at all aspects of defence. The testimony of men like Lieutenant General Moncel, Air Marshal Annis, Lieutenant General Fleury, Air Chief Marshal Miller and many others has left doubt in the minds of many about the value of the bill and about where we are heading.
There are those, including the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres who spoke on Friday, who say that this debate has taken too long. They forget that parliament is a place for discussion. Hon. members on this side have been participating in discussion, in a debate. Hon. members have been expressing their doubts and have been giving their views about this matter.
Everyone has agreed that integration is a good thing and I congratulate the minister for bringing it in because I think it was a forward step. Integration, however, had been under study for many years. The department had considered it for a long time and had carried out, as I have said, extensive studies. The minister implemented those studies. He also explained that integration was experimental, that errors would be made and that we shall not have the full benefits for some time to come. In that context I would think it would be better to wait until we can see the full
April 10. 1967
effects of the integration program before proceeding farther. It was said when integration was introduced that there would be a saving of many millions of dollars. I do not doubt that some savings were effected but they were not as great as Canadians had been led to believe.
Coming from an area in which there are two defence establishments and living in a town in which there is an R.C.A.F. station, Gimli, now known as Canadian Forces Base, Gimli, I have been over the years and am still much interested in the defence of our country. I might say in passing that we have had exceptionally good commanding officers throughout the years. We have been very fortunate in the high quality of these men and we have always enjoyed excellent public relations in our district between servicemen and civilians.
People in the services have expressed many doubts about this bill. Some, in common with some hon. members here, are in favour of it; others, in common with other hon. members here, are opposed to it. We are reaching the point where many in the services are afraid of saying anything against the bill as too many have been fired for speaking against it. Surely both views ought to be heard particularly from the minister's department. Everyone ought to be allowed to speak freely.
I do not agree with senior officers making speeches and statements to the public, as reported in this morning's Montreal Gazette. The article is headed "Unification Defended". The text reads as follows:
Vice-Admiral R. L. Hennessy Friday night delivered a spirited broadside at critics of armed forces unification in an address to the Navy League of Canada.
"The myth that unification will destroy the navy isn't borne out by the facts," he said.
"It verges on being insulting to the fine men of the navy."
Those who say navy morale is low are either "ill-informed or misinformed."
The evidence before the committee showed that morale in the navy is at an all-time low; yet here is a senior officer saying that is not so. One of the reasons for hurrying this bill through is that if it is not passed morale in the armed forces will sink. As this officer says morale is high, there is no need to rush the bill.
While referring to freedom of speech I wish to read from an article in the Winnipeg Free 23033-931J
National Defence Act Amendment Press of Thursday, April 6, 1967. The column is headed "Who Can Speak?". It says:
Defence Minister Paul Hellyer's staff play under some peculiar ground rules when it comes to speaking out in public.
In Parliament on Monday, when opposition members questioned some statements that General Jean Allard, the chief of staff, was alleged to have made in a speech in Montreal, Mr. Hellyer sprang quickly to his defence. (The fact that General Allard was misquoted has no bearing on this particular point, as Mr. Hellyer admitted he did not know what the general had said.) What Mr. Hellyer said in the House was, "Mr. Speaker, I did not know of the speech, but I have complete confidence in the chief of the defence staff and he is at complete liberty to express himself publicly as he sees fit."
Does General Allard have this privilege because he is the chief of staff? Or does he have it because his views on unification coincide with Mr. Hellyer's? If it is proper for the general to express himself publicly as he sees fit, surely this should be extended to other senior military officers. But what happened to Lieutenant General Moncel, Rear Admiral Landymore, Lieutenant General Frank Fleury, Vice Admiral Kenneth Dyer and other senior officers when they questioned Mr. Hellyer's policies? They were fired out of hand.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Nonsense, says the minister? I hope that those senior officers enjoy that freedom in speaking that we enjoy in parliament.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The Minister of Transport told us the other day that it was important to hear both sides of the question. I hope, therefore, that this freedom exists and that the promotion of men who expressed their views will not be prevented. If this has taken place it is certainly cause for a great deal of alarm.
Canada is a member of NORAD and NATO and it is important that her military role should be integrated with defence and foreign policies. In addition, I certainly think that Canada's military organization should be able to fit in with the military arrangements of allies such as the United States and Britain. Last fall I had the opportunity to visit defence establishments in the United States on a NATO trip. Most of the information we received was classified and I will certainly not refer to it here. I will merely say that at all the bases we visited, whether navy, air force or marine corps, the commanding officer was always a four-star general and in every case, I would say, he was roughly 50 years of age. The minister said we should not be listening to senior officers such as these but that we should be paying attention to the younger men. Nevertheless these are the people upon whom Mr. McNamara relies for his ad-

April 10, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment vice-the senior officers at these bases and at the Pentagon. I think it is indispensable that any minister should have the benefit of advice from people who have made the defence of their country a lifetime job.
I have put forward the view that our forces should be similar in structure to those of the United States and Britain. I found no indication that the United States was contemplating any change in the present constitution of its services, that is, an army, a navy and an air force. I should like to quote part of an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, a paper which is a strong supporter of the Liberal party though it has often come out with editorials directed against the present government. This editorial says:
As members of parliament cast their votes in support or rejection of Mr. Hellyer's bill, they must surely recognize the grave responsibility they bear individually. It is a question that ^ far transcends both politicking and party. Canadians will not lightly forgive or forget if our defence structure is thoughtlessly dismembered. This ill-advised step could, by a single act of parliament, sponsored by an inexperienced minister, tear down and destroy proven services which have been built with the sacrifice and efforts of Canadians in the past hundred years and more.
The reputation, character, efficiency and traditions of Canada's regular and militia units have been won and tested in action in battlefields in Europe, Asia and Africa, in the sea lanes of the North Atlantic and in the bombing and fighter missions in the air. They have been carefully designed and organized to work in the closest possible harmony with our two major allies, Great Britain and the United States.
It is beyond comprehension that Mr. Hellyer, by insisting on total unification, should ask parliament now to endorse a completely new defence structure, entirely foreign to both British and U.S. defence organizations. Unification, and elimination of service identities, despite Mr. Hellyer's statements to the contrary, have been openly rejected by Britain after much study-as declared in the white paper of 1963. A check with Washington would also reveal that the U.S. has no intention of unifying its combat units. To the contrary, the present purpose is to build up the proud reputations and esprit de corps of individual fighting units, whether it be the "Green Berets", the Marines or the first Cavalry Regiment. For Canada to launch into a radical experiment which will make our defence organization incompatible with U.S. and British organization constitutes the most drastic step ever taken with the defences of this country. It could, in large measure, destroy our existing defence structure.
Bearing this in mind, I say that the minister should be extremely careful, when contemplating changes in the defence structure of Canada, to see that our forces fit into the defence structures of the United States and Great Britain.

Furthermore, the NATO agreement is to be reviewed in 1968 to arrive at a basis for the coming ten years and the indications are that great changes will be brought about. At this point I should like to read from another article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on April 4:
In the course of the next year, Canada will be reviewing and renegotiating her military commitments under NATO. Common sense, at least, should dictate delaying any major revision of our defence forces until these revised undertakings become known.
Regiments, air squadrons and ships' companies are not simply constructed by bookkeeping statistics, mechanical devices, theories on paper, or by inexperienced guesswork. Canada has much practical experience to draw on. It should not be ignored. A far more cautious and realistic approach should be adopted before risking the destruction of such matters as confidence, harmony, pride of service, esprit de corps and proud tradition which every great commander in history has recognized as the vital qualities in any fighting service. Such things, when destroyed, cannot easily or quickly be restored.
In considering this bill in parliament, members should demand some explanation of the effect of Mr. Hellyer's program on Canada's important commitments under NATO and NORAD. These continuing responsibilities should not be ducked or diverted to buy support for Mr. Hellyer's unification program.
As has been pointed out, if Canada's role is to be merely one of peacekeeping, unification could perhaps be justified. But if we are to have a force of the kind which has existed in the past there can certainly be no justification for such a drastic step. I notice that even though integration was begun some two years ago the estimates for 1967-68 are roughly $115 million higher than the defence estimates for 1966-67. The total estimates of the department for the present year amount roughly to $1,600 million. This is an enormous amount of money. Members of this committee are entitled to know, as are the people of Canada, exactly what the defence forces of this country consist of. Most of the editorials which have appeared in the press are strongly opposed to the bill we are now discussing. Last night I listened to a television program in the course of which Charles Lynch said he felt the debate in this house was justified because in his opinion this was a dangerous bill and one which should be opposed. I am sure the minister has read editorials in papers right across Canada, every one of them condemning the bill before us and suggesting it would be most unwise to move hastily at this time.

In conclusion I wish to propose some questions to the minister. Will the passing of this

bill save the people of Canada money, or has the minister some doubts about this? Will the passing of this bill assure Canada of an effective defence force, or has the minister some doubts about this? Is insistence on a single uniform not likely to have an effect on the morale of the forces? If it does affect morale would it not be better to allow the three services to retain their identities by retaining their respective uniforms? Has the testimony given by many qualified personnel as to their doubts about the bill not been a shock to the minister and left some doubts in his mind?
I find myself having serious doubts about these points, and if the minister has any doubts I hope he will proceed with caution and take another look at what this bill may achieve. He has indicated that it will take many years to implement the provisions of the bill. Therefore there does not seem to be any need for rush. I believe at this particular moment we are running ahead of public opinion, and running so far ahead of it in this effort at unification that the public will neither understand nor support unification.
Public reaction, both from those who had a smattering of military knowledge and from those who wanted to save money, was favourable to integration. People agreed in general with the fact that we could integrate support, supply and command services and thereby produce a more effective national fighting force at more modest cost. This was the first thing which the public approved, but I am going to submit that the public's view has changed and that the minister cannot ignore this change or, if he does, it will be at his peril.
The second thing the public felt was that unification, the second step of integration as they saw it, was not really understood by any civilian. However, they felt the minister had assurances from his experts that everyone in the services knew what was involved and everyone in the services approved. On this basis the public went along with the question of unification believing that though they could not understand it everybody else did. There was no effective vocal opposition across the country. But that public reaction has changed.

I should like to say, from my own very limited experience, that morale and esprit de corps are very intangible things. They cannot be photographed like a uniform; they cannot be counted like individual members of the service; they cannot be valued like equipment. They are, however, eminently more important than any of these things. The absence of a willingness to work together with another group, the absence of a pride in one's own unit, and the absence of pride in one's own service, take away all the desire of a fighting man to do a little better. All the great stories of military adventures have arisen because some member of a unit has done something which has brought that unit to the attention of others and has given it a special importance. The unit perhaps has led an attack or held the line and many of the personnel in that unit receive medals. These are the important things which are involved in morale.
Medical men tell us that shock often is the cause of death of persons who are involved in an accident. It is difficult either to define or distinguish shock. It can be caused by loss of blood or by injury. Sometimes it is caused by a combination of several things. The result of shock, however, can be death just as definitely as decapitation. In many cases the real cause of death never can be defined. I am attempting to establish that shock easily could cause the death of the Canadian armed forces if the fighting men should lose their morale and esprit de corps.
There seems to be a feeling that unification is based on some changed concept in respect of the defence of Canada or in respect of the methods of waging war. This new concept has not been defined by the minister and therefore we are left guessing as to what is behind the need for unification of the forces. Some people believe that the advent of a most horrible means of mass destruction will eliminate the likelihood of a conventional war or conventional battles. Of course, all the evidence is to the contrary. The battles which are going on at the present time are in the conventional war field.
I can remember that in the 1930's, prior to the second world war, we were told that if there should be another world war it might be the end of mankind. People gave as an example all the various types of gases which were available in great quantities. They told us about the germs which were being incubated in thousands of places. It was said that if war broke out these germs would be released and everybody would be wiped out. This did not
April 10, 1987	COMMONS
happen. When members of the armed forces went into battle in the second world war, for months they carried respirators or gas masks and then later these were abandoned. In fact, even in his death throes and his final instability Hitler did not authorize the use of mass destruction.
I do not believe we should assume that there would be no conventional attack on this country, that there would be no conventional war, or that we would have nothing to meet of a conventional standard. I believe this is what we are doing and that we are laying a false basis, but I am not sure in what direction the minister is moving because this has never been explained. We really cannot tell in what direction the government is moving.
I should like to conclude my remarks with a word of advice to the minister. He may not wish to take it but I think he should. I know he has received much advice in the past few months but he has not received any from me previously.

and has made some sort of estimate of the cost. If it has made such an estimate, I suggest such an estimate would make it perfectly obvious that we cannot create a mobile intervention force and maintain our existing roles, within the budget ceiling that we now have.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that if we cling to the existing roles in NATO, unification makes no sense. There is an inevitable conclusion to be drawn from this, and in this respect I agree with the official opposition although not with their ultimate conclusion. The inevitable conclusion to be drawn is that the government does not mean what it says when it asserts, on the one hand, that it is going to proceed with unification with all speed and, on the other, that it is going to maintain its present roles.
It is my view that the explanation of this matter is to be found in a careful examination of the speech last Wednesday, of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is a disciple, and a very apt one, of his former leader, the late Mr. Mackenzie King. Mr. Mackenzie King, when he spoke on external affairs-some of us are old enough to remember his speeches and to have looked at them carefully-was able to keep everyone happy. This was done by studied obscurity, by never saying clearly what course of action or what school of thought the government favoured. Included in his speeches in the house was one section which seemed to favour Canadian isolation from European wars, another support for the commonwealth, and another devotion to the ideals of collective security exemplified by the League of Nations. No doubt if there were any other significant elements of opinion they would be found duly recorded, rather vaguely and hazily perhaps, in the speeches made by the then prime minister. Every significant trend of Canadian public opinion would find its views somewhere contained in the announcement of Canadian policy. Then the experts used to get to work and analyse the different, inconsistent streams of thought that appeared in Mr. King's utterances, try to determine which predominated and guess Canadian policy therefrom.

I think that the ghost of Mr. King still rules the government which has adopted his style. Therefore I do not find it so surprising that the intentions of the government with regard to its future relations with NATO are wrapped in obscurity. It is quite prepared to adopt a
