sweeping organizational change in the Canadian armed services, which would only-make sense if we were to change our roles in the future, and at the same time to assert stoutly its devotion to the maintenance of its present roles in NATO which do not at all fit into the new organizational structure.
However, in this light I studied the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs very carefully and I may claim by now, having been in the house five years and having followed the words of the minister very carefully, to be an expert Martinologist, if I may coin a word. As a result of my studies I think I have resolved the mystery. It is perfectly true that the Secretary of State for External Affairs in one part of his speech does indeed appear to assert firmly the intention of maintaining unchanged Canada's present role in NATO. But then I find at the top of page 14565 of Hansard the following statement:
I do not exclude the possibility that in the future it may become feasible, and indeed I hope it will, to withdraw our forces from Europe and to make our entire contribution from bases in Canada. But such a course of action is neither feasible nor desirable at this moment, and certainly not by unilateral decision.
It is my suggestion that the key words in this utterance are "at this moment". The organizational structure of our armed forces must not be considered in the light of what is current at the moment but in the light of the future, and in the light of the future can there be any doubt at all that the government intends to change its role in NATO? I suggest that is the key to this seeming conundrum of a government which proposes a sweeping change in organization and at the same time refuses to announce policies which would make sense of this sweeping change. I think it is quite right for the government to consider the future. What I think is wrong is to conceal from the people of Canada its true intent. No responsible government can propose the continuance of roles which are no longer militarily useful, necessary or sensible.

Mr. Chairman, few debates ever held in this chamber have had more critical significance for Canada's future than that in which we are engaged. Yet at this stage it is not easy to present any novel or original arguments. For myself, I have never professed that knowledge of defence or matters military which would qualify me to speak with confident authority. On the other hand, sir, that very lack of expertise may have enabled me to approach the issue of unification of our armed forces with a completely objective view. I have been able to examine the evidence given in the standing committee without preconceived bias, and I have certainly done so without political partisanship.
To the study of that evidence I have given agonizing care. This detailed study of the evidence before the standing committee on defence has convinced me that this bill ought not to be enacted and has convinced me that if it is enacted it will irreparably damage the national interest. Indeed, sir, I fail to see how any objective person reading the evidence could come to any other conclusion. While I have spent many hours analysing and annotating the evidence before the committee, I see no particular point in spreading it further on the record. I will abbreviate my speech at least in that respect.
Nor do I think it is necessary or desirable to attack the integrity or bona tides of any witness. Most of the evidence presented to the committee was opinion evidence, and any experienced barrister knows how widely such evidence may differ even when tendered by equally sincere witnesses. But, sir, overwhelmingly the weight of evidence tendered by those who were free to speak without any inhibition was in opposition to this bill. I say to you, sir, that for parliament to act in the face of the opinions which were expressed by Air Chief Marshal Miller, General Guy Si-monds and General Robert Moncel would be irresponsible and foolhardy in the extreme. It

National Defence Act Amendment is all very well to say that there are other opinions of a contrary nature and to assert that the government and parliament have a responsibility to act.
My submission, which I want to make tonight directly to the Prime Minister, is simply-I make it to the Prime Minister because in my view he is the only man who can save Canada's present armed forces from annihilation-that administration and no parliament can properly disregard such expert opinion as that of Miller, Simonds, Moncel, Curtis and many others. No administration and no parliament should jeopardize the safety and security of a nation in the face of the opinions of such men.
I say to the Prime Minister that the task of statescraft is to achieve a national consensus, and where there is not a reasonable national consensus upon a fundamental issue affecting the very life of the nation then no action or at least delayed action is to be preferred to hasty and indigestible action. That is the very essence of statescraft. I assert to the Prime Minister that in my view this nation is not ready for unification and he should draw back before irreparable damage is done. This is not a matter merely of someone winning an argument. This is not just a case of the majority in parliament having its way. This bill is a blow at the very heart of our future as a nation. As Prime Minister the right hon. gentleman from Algoma East has a positive and unequivocal duty to all Canada to reconsider this hasty and ill-conceived measure. He was not sworn in as Her Majesty's first minister in order to preside over the liquidation of Canada's armed forces.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Sir, no one here doubts the desirability of what has come to be described as integration-integration of support services and a measure of consolidation of command. However, the destruction of service traditions, the dynamiting of all unit loyalties in order to create a single force, is another matter. In my view it ought not to be done. It certainly ought not to be done without the clear, unequivocal mandate of the Canadian people. I assert that only the Canadian people have the right to take the chances with the survival of the nation which are implicit in this bill. The Minister of National Defence claims to be leading the world on the road to unification. Personally, I would feel a great deal happier if other nations showed any disposition to follow; I detect none. In fact, the minister is leading a one-man parade. His attempts to
14736	COMMONS DEBATES	April 10. 1967
National Defence Act Amendment gain the support of Admiral Mountbatten backfired over last week end and the explanations made by the minister this afternoon were totally unrealistic. Informed opinion in Britain, the United States and throughout the world indicates, I think, total disenchantment with the proposals that are implicit in this bill.
On Thursday last, Mr. Chairman, as reported at page 14592 of Hansard, the Associate Minister of National Defence professed to speak for all servicemen. He went on to say that he believed the forces are convinced that the goal of unification is correct. I believe that few statements ever made in this house have infuriated more people. Since that statement was made, Mr. Chairman, I have literally been besieged by messages, both identified and anonymous, from servicemen in my riding protesting against the arrogance of the associate minister in professing to speak for all servicemen, and asserting with what I believe is constitutional propriety that only the member that they elect can profess to speak in parliament for any citizen, civilian or serviceman.
The associate minister may profess to speak for the servicemen in the constituency of Terrebonne, but he has no mandate to speak for the servicemen in the constituency of Carleton. I would remind the committee that only the members for Halifax and the hon. member for Russell have as many service electors as I have in Carleton. From the representations made to me, I am convinced that the overwhelming number of my service constituents and their dependants share the views that I am expressing tonight.
However, sir, I do not believe that it is a matter of counting service heads. It is a matter of judgment. My judgment and my submission is that the Prime Minister should intervene now to withdraw this bill, and I plead with him to do so. My observations, both of my service constituents and otherwise, are that the operational efficiency of our armed forces has been brought to its lowest point. Destruction of service loyalties and abandonment of historic units cannot help but lower morale, and that is precisely what has happened. The situation today is that our armed forces are being used as a pawn in the struggle for the Liberal leadership, and the Prime Minister should put an end to it at once.
In my view, Mr. Chairman, the provisions of this bill constitute a direct breach of faith with all serving officers and men. They enlisted upon one basis; this bill shifts the ground

rules completely without any right of election to the servicemen. Legally of course this can be done. Morally it is indefensible. When we come to the particular clause in the bill I shall have more to say on the subject.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I venture to direct my words immediately to the attention of the Prime Minister. Into his hands, the fourteenth man so privileged in 100 years of confederation, has come the chief responsibility for the safety and integrity of the nation. I submit to him that the issue before this parliament is too basic, too essential, to the national future to be determined over the protests of the outstanding Canadians who have given their lives to service in the armed forces. In fact, this bill has reached its present stage only by the purge of almost all senior military advisers to the nation, a purge more ruthless than anything ever attempted by anyone anywhere since Stalin's purge of the red army.
I repeat with all the emphasis at my command that the essence of statescraft is to give leadership in the achievement of a reasonable national consensus. This the bill cannot do. Normally the task of parliament is to exercise judgment and to make decisions. This bill transcends that and ought not to be implemented, in my view, without the direct mandate of the people.
If the Prime Minister persists in enacting this bill, then let at least clause 65 be amended to provide that the bill shall come into force only 90 days or 120 days after the next election. In saying that, Mr. Chairman, I am not advocating an early election. Indeed I believe that a bitterly fought election on the eve of our centennial celebrations would be undesirable. But no harm would come about if this bill is postponed a year or two or more. Indeed, I am convinced that much good would result from delay.
The Prime Minister was prepared, Mr. Chairman, to delay medicare, even at the expense of losing the Minister of National Health and Welfare from the cabinet. Despite the risk of his losing the Minister of National Defence from the cabinet-and may I confess to believing that the loss would be a heavensent blessing-let the Prime Minister agree to delay this bill. Then whenever the next election comes-be it one year or two years away, or whenever it may be-the people will have the opportunity to pass upon a proposal which in its present form, in my view, now endangers the very life of our nation. The people of Canada can take the risk of endangering the survival of the nation: My submission is that this parliament cannot.
April 10. 1967

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first words in opening the second part of a speech that I began a week ago are helpful to the morale of the minister. I want to assure him right off the bat that in any conflict between statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra and the Minister of National Defence I would go along with the Minister of National Defence.
The second compliment I should like to pay him is to thank him for the continuation of the hydrofoil program. I think the announcement that he made in answer to a question I raised a week ago has done a considerable amount to help the morale of the armed forces in the constituency of Halifax. It does show there is some hope that the minister, no matter what his shortcomings-and heaven only knows they have been combed over from right to left and from north to south in recent days in this chamber-means to keep the Royal Canadian Navy in business.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I referred to the statements made earlier today by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra because he would have us believe that anything going on here is but a simple exercise in name changing, that we were really spending an extraordinary amount of time bringing about this change in name. The hon. member also had unkind words to say about certain hon. members on this side, suggesting they had not really read the minutes of the defence committee he headed. Having heard his speech I suggest that he neither heard nor understood what was said in that committee. I refer to the remarks of the Minister of National Defence, in which he deals with what he considers an imperative need to get along with this bill. On the second column of page 14438 of Hansard the minister said this:
The passage of this bill does not mean instant unification. The passage of this bill is a statement of the intention that the ultimate goal is a single service and all the men and women in the forces will be managed in a single personnel stream. This must be known in order that the kind of detailed staff planning required can proceed on an orderly basis.
Comparing that statement with the utterances of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra one would think that there was more to this bill than a mere change of name. Indeed, should the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra look at the bill-and I invite him to do so-he will find that in clause 2 a change is to be made to section 15 of the National Defence Act, setting up one service to be known as the Canadian Armed Forces. That of course
National Defence Act Amendment is a change of name, but it involves the process of unification. In clause 4 there is something dealing with the naming of ranks, and in clause 6 the members of the armed forces will become members of the Canadian Armed Forces. Here again there is more than just a change of name.
Clause 7 softens part of clause 6, removing the possibility that a person who has entered service in the army, navy or air force will be conscripted to duties which were alien to him in a single service. Having said these things, I think we can safely dispose of the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra that all we are dealing with here is a change in name.
I also wish to be kind to the minister, though briefly. I shall not change my nature entirely. A very good suggestion, appearing at first blush to support the minister, comes from Major General F. F. "Fighting Frank" Worthington, who said this:
As one of Canada's oldest generals it Is my opinion that at the end of any large war the existing generals should be thanked, decorated and pensioned off.
Put up statues if you like, but don't let them meddle with the future organization of the services. Hand that responsibility over to the young, fighting colonels who had to fight the war with the existing weapons.
It seems to me, as one reads between the lines, that the Minister of National Defence ought to pay attention to the views of the fighting colonels, the hon. members for Calgary North and Winnipeg South Centre, two excellent and knowledgeable persons to whom I hope the minister pays attention.
The strongest indictment of the minister's proposal is that it asks us to do something, and we do not really know what it is. We suspect the minister does not know either. Nevertheless he is asking for parliament to give him carte blanche to bring about some new process involving the national defence of the country.
Earlier in the debate I quoted extensively from the evidence of Air Chief Marshal Miller. Passing over some significant portions dealing with my point, I turn to page 2300 of the committee minutes, where the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona is asking this of the air chief marshal:
If I have your testimony correct, unification had been talked about but you had never seen or heard the implications of it spelled out. Is that accurate?
Air Chief Marshal Miller: We never had tentative unification plans submitted and agreed to.
April 10, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment The air chief marshal was chief of the defence staff, a position he held for two years covering a large part of the present minister's ministry. The air chief marshal perforce, one would think, would be the minister's closest adviser, and privy to his thoughts. He would be in the position of an adviser to the minister. The air chief marshal vacated that post in July or August of last summer.
On November 4 the Bill C-243 is presented to us in its present form. That bill has not just one page, as one would expect if it dealt only with a change of name, but has 48 pages in all, including the various schedules. It was not prepared overnight; as a lawyer I know that it would take weeks or months of preparation. The inference I am trying to draw-and I do not think one can be drawn to the contrary-is that the unification bill was prepared in the Department of National Defence without the leading officer of the department, the chief of the defence staff, having had an opportunity to know what it would deal with. If he had any inkling, there was no exchange of opinions between himself and the minister about the different parts of the unification concept. I find this almost unbelievable.
Any other minister bringing in something as radically new as this bill would have had an exchange of views with his deputy minister and leading officials of the department. Papers would have been prepared; the subject would have been discussed around the water coolers in various government departments. Why did this not happen here? I will repeat that part of the testimony where at page 2300, the air chief marshal says:
We never had tentative unification plans submitted and agreed to.
I think those words were amplified in other parts of his testimony.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Here we have a massive 48-page bill dealing with unification, produced a few months after Air Chief Marshal Miller had left that office. It defies all common sense and all logic that any minister of the crown should proceed in such a fashion. Even trying to give the minister the benefit of any possible doubt, I find it impossible to believe that there could have been any thinking going into the unification concept which lies behind this measure. It could not have grown up overnight in the month or two before Bill C-243 was drafted. I hope I live long enough for somebody to write a book and explain just how this miracle could be possible. I hope it will not be the [Mr. McCleave.l

gospel according to St. Paul but that some independent observer will explain this miracle to my satisfaction.
There are one or two points which puzzle me in connection with the specific details of unification. One of them is the failure to spell out in simple form, or even in complicated form, the ordinary day to day life of a serviceman so that it would be understandable to those who are trying to grapple with this concept.
For example, nothing has been said about the type of uniform he will wear, the type of living quarters he will occupy, the possibility of his being taken from one kind of duty, in a tank, for instance, and put on another kind of duty, perhaps supporting those who are operating in an air environment. Boiling it down in my own mind, take the case of a young fellow who wants to be a cook in the services. He goes to an integrated recruiting station, which of course exists at the present time, and may be cajoled into going to sea to cook, when all his instincts are against this; he would much prefer to cook at a stationary base, or even for a field unit serving in a ground environment-and I apologize for using some of the older terms. But who on earth would want to be served food at sea by a seasick cook?
There are other examples. I am advised that in the Royal Canadian Navy they do not want men much over the age of 40 to embark on vessels, life at sea being what it is. They feel that only the rare person over 40 who has good physical stamina should be allowed to continue a career which would keep him in a sea environment. Again-and I am relying on advice given to me by professionals-this is not the case with those serving in the air force or the army. They may not want senior officers or older men to handle planes, but I understand that the age requirement is not so restrictive. On this point I should like the minister to tell us just how unification would take into account the different approaches which the services use toward their personnel.
Last week I mentioned the case in Halifax of a person who under the present integration process could not find out who his immediate superior was. Other cases have come to my attention in the Halifax area. The transportation services of the three armed forces have been integrated, and this seems to have quadrupled the number of people engaged in transportation, most of them occupied in writing memoranda to each other without any
April 10, 1967	COMMONS
increase in the number of motor vehicles being driven about. I suppose this is inevitable; it is bound to happen when you take a large department and attempt to reorganize it. I do not minimize the problem the minister faces on this regard, because he has a $1.5 billion operation to look after, and it is difficult to make changes in it. But seeing the Parkinsonian laws in operation following the integration of transportation facilities for the armed forces in the Halifax area, one wonders how effective these plans are and how quickly any bugs can be ironed out.
Finally, I should like to make four points concerning the course which I respectfully suggest the minister should follow. I see it is almost seven o'clock, so perhaps I could wind up my speech at 8 p.m. and make them then-it will take about five minutes.

Mr. Chairman, in my remarks before the dinner hour I had indicated that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, chairman of the defence committee during its final sessions, appeared to have been there in body and not in mind, and was unaware of the implications of Bill C-243 which we are now considering. I suggested to the Minister of National Defence that at some time an attempt be made to spell out as simply as possible, so that even he could understand, just what was meant by his concept of unification, and what it would mean in the practical day to day living of members of the Canadian Armed Forces.
Also before the dinner hour we heard an outstanding speech and plea by the hon. member for Carleton, mainly directed to the Prime Minister who has the paramount interest and authority with regard to this matter. I could only very humbly second the very forceful, eloquent and wise words of the hon. member for Carleton. I hope that the Prime Minister, who seemed to grasp the nettle a few weeks ago by expressing surprise and interest at the remarks of Air Chief Marshal Miller, will
National Defence Act Amendment again come to grips with the subject and exercise the responsibility that is his.
Finally, sir, I would like at this time to make four suggestions to the Minister of National Defence as to the course he could follow. The first is that I think it is necessary that integration be made to work. Integration is the expressed will of the parliament of Canada. There has been considerable evidence given before the defence committee about the snafus, the bugs, the serious problems that have cropped up in the Department of National Defence, and I understand most of these relate to the process of integration.
If the first step, integration, is not a completely successful one, why on earth should we in this committee expect that the further step of unification should be a successful one? The Minister of National Defence makes the point that it is necessary to have something on the statute books so that integration can be carried a step further into the area of unification. If this be so, and I take the word of the minister that it is so, then I suggest this step as a corollary to point No. 1, namely an amendment to section 18 of the present National Defence Act which would permit units of one service to join other services. I think in this way experimentation of a useful nature could be carried out, and the minister could iron out the bugs and develop his concept with a small unification scheme, rather than starting in with over-all unification.
I have made my second point in a previous contribution to this debate so I will not dwell on it at any length, but I wish to say I was very much impressed to see the service battalion in operation at Camp Gagetown a number of years ago. I think the minister and the officials of his department would be taking the right course were they to continue to fit the non-combatant units and non-combatant services together in support of the three services. My third point, dealing with unification, has to do with my first point concerning making integration work and attempting unification on a more humble scale. I think we should have some proof, and probably evidence given before an all-party committee on national defence, before the full plunge into unification is made.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
My fourth and final point is in the area of high speculation and opinion. However, in this debate everyone has entered into this field. As other hon. members have so well pointed out, we are largely in the field of opinion when we deal with this matter.
14740	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment
It seems to me that if the minister's philosophy is correct and if all the developments in national defence here and in other countries are to be assessed correctly, we have had a significant move in this century, probably as a result of the nuclear age. It may be that the days of large-scale citizen armies are over. We have gone through a period of approximately 200 years when countries as a whole have been at war; and now, because of the nuclear age, we are coming into a period when small, professional and highly mobile services are necessary. Perhaps this is illustrated by the fact that the minister has closed down a number of the militia units which had been in existence in Canada for a long time.
I suggest to the minister, that, keeping in mind the holocaust a nuclear war would bring, the logical extension of what he has been doing would be to take even further steps in developing a closer bond between the services and those who are not in the services.
I believe the thinking today would suggest that the civilian population could become more involved in emergency matters than in military matters; that is, we would still rely on the small professional force, but the citizens who are not members of the services would have to carry out the measures which are necessary for the survival of the population.
This type of development, horrendous though it might appear, is consistent with the realities of the nuclear age. I do not believe we should continue to think in terms of the 1914-1918 and the 1939-1949 era. The Emergency Measures Organization should be further developed in order that it will be in readiness to step in instantly, in a time of emergency, so that the people can be mobilized-not in the military sense-in an effort to survive.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make an appeal to the minister to pay some heed to the advice which has been offered and the questions which have been asked from this side of the chamber. National defence really is too important a matter to be either a partisan issue or one which develops as a result of one person's style of thinking. As other hon. members have pointed out, heretofore unification itself had never come before the retired chief of the defence staff in a tangible form and in a form which would have entitled us to raise questions concerning exactly what the minister had in mind. Until we have knowledge of what he has in mind we are entitled to ask questions on behalf of all the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I was happy to hear the hon. member for Halifax wind up with a reminder of the importance of this debate. I thought the hon. member for Carleton brought that very forcibly to the fore. It seems necessary to comment on some of the incredible speeches made in this house by hon. members across the way. I found the remarks made by the Minister of Transport on Friday remarkable in more ways than one, and I intend to get around to them later. Also the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra made an incredible speech this afternoon, for one who was chairman of the committee. During the committee hearings I did not think he had any realization of what was going on, but I did not expect such a frank expose of the depth of the ignorance he had concerning what was involved as he exhibited this afternoon. I will also comment on that.
One suggestion which was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood I think should be developed by what is possibly a logical extension of his reasoning. I found myself quite unable to disagree with the arguments he put forward when he mentioned what the government is trying to do, so to speak, through the back door. He pointed out that the only way in which anyone could find a logical pattern in what the government is doing is to suggest that secretly they seem to have made up their minds that Canada must change its role in defence and world affairs. If I judge his remarks correctly, he has found this to be in the peace keeping role; that is, that the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs can be interpreted to mean only that Canada's commitments will be changed later this year, and that the present unification bill, the shape of the forces and the speeches made by the Minister of National Defence all form a pattern which indicates that Canada intends to drop or drastically change some of its commitments in respect of NATO and so on. It would seem that we are intending to put more emphasis on peacekeeping and that our foreign affairs policy in the near future will follow this pattern.
The hon. member for Greenwood deprecated the fact that the government was not being more frank with the members of the house and the people of Canada in revealing its intention. The only thing about which I quarrel with the hon. member is that I believe he may be counting too much on this government following a plan because certainly from what the Minister of National Defence has been doing it is obvious that the lack of a plan has
April 10, 1967	COMMONS
been the most disturbing thing to the members of the armed forces and to the nation in the last couple of years. Therefore perhaps the first mistake we make is in expecting to find some logical plan which the government is following.
It may be that the action they are taking makes so little sense that they are just as misguided and undirected as they appear to be. Certainly the hon. member for Greenwood is the only one who has attempted to search out what the government may be doing. I should like to point out that if he is right, then it occurs to us that our policy in respect of foreign affairs is being decided now by a change in our armed forces.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I am one of those who have always felt that the armed forces of Canada should be able to respond to the support of the policy of the government on external affairs as that policy may exist or be formed from time to time, that the only policy that makes sense is to keep our armed forces in such shape that they do not interfere with the ability of the country to be able to formulate or change its foreign policy, and that the armed forces should be able to give as much weight and credence as possible to the external affairs posture that we adopt. Therefore I am most disturbed at the thought that the hon. member for Greenwood may be right, and certainly the evidence indicates that he is, that what is happening today under this minister is that our armed forces are being tailored so that we can have only one possible sort of external affairs policy.
Up to this time I am sure that most people in the country have been perturbed at the thought that the minister is selling the country a bill of goods when he says that he has been giving us more defence for less money, and we have found the evidence to be that we are getting less and less defence for more money. Next we are disturbed at the thought of what he is doing to our armed forces, the amount of destruction and harm he is doing to them, senselessly, since there is no rhyme nor reason why he should be proceeding with unification, and certainly less reason why he should be proceeding with this program with such haste. This situation becomes even worse when we consider that the result is not just less defence for more money but we are going to lose our ability to manoeuvre in the field of external affairs. I am against external affairs being decided on the basis of defence policy, especially when it is sold under such false
National Defence Act Amendment pretences as the minister is using in attempting to sell it. I am even more against it if we are to be put in a strait-jacket that will determine our external affairs policy for years to come.
I think this is a fundamental point that the house should not overlook. At least with the old structure of the defence forces as we know them, we had freedom to move about in our defence policy as we wished. Many witnesses who appeared before the defence committee pointed out that it was perfectly possible and logical, and this had always been the case, for the government to decide external affairs policy and then, by selecting certain parts of our traditional armed forces, to make up any special units required to undertake any special tasks to which our external affairs policy committed us.
What is happening now is that we are going to make up a special type of force that will perhaps be most beneficial to one type of defence policy. What is more, we are destroying our traditional concept of the forces. We are destroying our three forces and substituting therefor a new and untried concept of one armed force, which it is hoped will be most useful in a new role in external affairs. The reversal of this process will be very, very difficult. We are not embarking on something that can be treated lightly. It is not an experiment, as are some of the experiments in integration, that can be reversed overnight if we find it is not working. If we allow this bill to pass and the government then proceeds to change its external affairs policy so that their new concept of an armed force makes sense, and we are to try that foreign affairs policy for two or three years and then change our minds and decide that we should find some other role or roles more in keeping with our status as a nation, more in keeping with our size or the feeling of the nation as to what we should be doing in world affairs, we will find ourselves in a strait-jacket. You cannot turn around and create a navy overnight, after it has disappeared for two or three years. You will not be able to create an air force as fast as you can destroy it.
The idea of having just one force because of the whim of this minister, in view of the way this concept has been presented in the house and the political attitude taken by government supporters, which will leave us in a strait-jacket for many years to come when it comes to external affairs policy, is something that just makes me sweat. I think the reminder of the hon member for Carleton was most
April 10, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment timely in his appeal to the Prime Minister. Every hon. member of the house should be reminded of this. It makes me very much afraid of what is happening in this house when I hear hon. members opposite say, "Let us get on with the job," and when I hear them approach this very serious problem of unification and its long-term effects on this country with the political arguments that they have used.
The Minister of National Defence has been telling us that integration-unification are one package, despite the overwhelming evidence that this is directly contrary to the truth. Hon. members on the other side of the house have used such political red herrings as to suggest that those who are against unification are against integration, are against modernization of our forces and are against progress.

How any member of parliament who takes his duties seriously and acts, as I believe a member should in this house, with some sort of honesty in regard to his duties, can state as his view such trash, in what should be a responsible speech, is quite beyond me. The hon. member for Leeds and one or two others on that side of the chamber followed exactly that policy, despite the wealth of the evidence to the contrary given by almost every witness who appeared before the defence committee that integration and unification are not one, that in fact integration is not one complete step at all, that each integration experiment is separate unto itself. I do not know how they can take this position, even with the assurance of General Allard, the chief of staff, who is for unification. The assurance of General Allard to the committee was that any step or any experiment in unification that does not work can be reversed. After that kind of clear evidence of how distinct and separate is each one of these experiments in integration, we still get this kind of nonsense from the minister and his blind followers on the other side of the house, namely that it is the integration-unification package that we are talking about today, and don't criticize unification or you are against progress.
If the mentality of hon. members opposite is of that standard, and if that is all they have learned after all the evidence that so many very able men gave to the defence committee, they should not be in this House of Commons, because either their intelligence is so weak or
[Mr. Nugent.l
their integrity is so lacking that they are very badly misplaced here.
I hope I have time to deal with the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, because it was a dandy. I did want to comment on the speech made by the Minister of Transport, since he is a very old and experienced member of this house-perhaps I should have said, since he is a very experienced elder member of this house-and one would normally expect to take what he says rather seriously. This, in essence, is what I gathered from his remarks: First, that we did not have to follow the advice of the experts on military affairs; that since we are breaking new ground and it is a new experiment, anybody's opinion is as good as anyone else's. That sounds to me an incredible approach to take, one that I did not think would be taken by anyone old enough to have graduated from school, and certainly not one in keeping with a man who holds a responsible portfolio in government, as does the Minister of Transport.
But the Minister of Transport pressed on with that theme. To give hon. members an illustration of how peculiar the thinking can get when one starts by saying we must defend the program, rather than logically arguing its faults or merits I would quote the following exchange as recorded on page 14670 of Hansard for April 7:

speechtext: Is the minister maintaining that the evidence does not prove anything?

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
I am maintaining that if the witnesses on the one side of the case are allowed to speak and the witnesses on the other side are inhibited by the rule from speaking all the evidence will be on one side. That is all I am saying.
April 10. 1967	COMMONS
Then I asked the minister a question, and the gist of his reply was that since no evidence was given on the order side we should discount the evidence given by the independent witnesses, such as Lieutenant Generals Fleury and Moncel, who were free to speak.
I want to review for a minute the situation in that committee. We asked for all the evidence from all the witnesses, all the senior officers who were now free to speak and who had been in the armed forces since the inception of the integration program. We wanted to hear them all, so that we could get a consensus of what went on. We were balked at every turn by members on the Liberal side. We asked for many more witnesses than we were able to get. To get any of them was like pulling teeth.
If there had been any officers who had reached the normal retirement age or who had retired early who were in favour of unification, I am sure there would have been no objection to hearing their evidence from anyone on the Conservative side of the house. We wanted to get all the evidence from all of those who were in a position to give us their expert advice, who had knowledge of the situation and knowledge of the facts, and who were now free to speak. What the Minister of Transport said is that since the only ones who were free to speak were against unification we must ignore their evidence because, according to his reasoning their evidence does not mean anything. I suppose he accepted my argument that those who are still in the forces must simply follow the government's policy, and we are unable to get their private and personal opinion. He sums it up by saying that only those in the department who are inhibited from speaking freely are in favour of unification, that the only ones who spoke against it are from outside the department, and that therefore we have called only witnesses on one side of the argument.
As I attempted to suggest to him in my question, surely if there are people who are free to speak and who believe in unification they would have come. Would the Liberals not have called them before the committee if there were any such people? Surely they must have had some officers in the positions of Lieutenant Generals Fleury and Moncel and Air Marshal Annis who would have come forward and backed up the minister in his ridiculous stand on this question. Is it wrong for this house to conclude that because the only witnesses who were free to speak all spoke against unification there is nobody free to speak who is in favour of unification? This
National Defence Act Amendment is the logical deduction which I would make from the failure of the proponents of unification to produce one free agent to speak on their behalf. When I say "one free agent" I must qualify it by saying that a couple of witnesses who appeared before the committee were in favour of unification, but most of them were out of touch with the services. General Foulkes spoke on both sides; and there was another independent witness, long removed from the services. But I think I am accurate in saying there was unanimous evidence before the committee given by those who were in the most responsible positions when the integration program was started, who were most intimately connected with what was going on in the forces and who were free to speak, that unification is wrong.
If some of them did not go quite so far as to say it was wrong, they certainly said it was wrong to proceed with it at this time. The most support the minister received was when some of them said that when the experiments with integration are completed, the results tried and tested, it might be found that unification would be a good thing and we might then introduce it. However, those are the kindest remark that the minister got from people who are in a position to know. Bearing that in mind, how can the assertion be made by so many hon. members on the other side that we should get on with the job, since integration and unification are one package? What nonsense.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, who was chairman of that committee, amazed me with his speech today. He said that all this bill does is to change the name of the forces. He certainly made a monkey out of those on the other side of the house who say it is necessary to pass the unification bill so that we can carry on the great work of integration, complete the modernization of our forces, streamline them and finish up the job started. As a matter of fact I thought this was the minister's theme song, this was his argument. The minister has been saying that it is all one package and that unification is necessary to complete the whole process. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra understands as well as I do that the minister's remark is a lot of hot air, because it is not all one process.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra told us that the bill on unification is not necessary. It is apparent that he has listened carefully to the evidence of the witnesses before the committee. I am afraid his financial arguments are a little confused because every
April 10. 1967

National Defence Act Amendment witness who came before the committee said that any saving which can result either from integration or unification will be the result of the integration process alone. They have all told us that unification will not save us money. Perhaps that is what the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra meant when he said that this bill is not necessary. He went on to say there would be no savings as a result of this bill. Certainly he demonstrated a degree of honesty which we wish the minister showed. It hurts me very much to hear the only member on the Liberal side being so honest about the financial aspect and so confused about the other aspects of unification, which makes his evidence on our behalf not very helpful.
This may be a little embarrassing to the minister, but that is the way that the chairman of that committee sees it after all those sittings. He said first that the bill is not necessary, second that unification will not save us money, and third that this bill does not affect the composition of the forces. This is a most remarkable statement; in fact I find it incredible. Here we have a bill, the sole purpose of which is to destroy the identity of the three separate forces as they now exist and substitute therefore the minister's brainchild of one force. In fact the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra is making light of this great achievement of the minister. He says that the bill does not affect the composition of the forces, and yet the Minister of National Defence says that this is a brilliant new concept, that Canada is now the leader of the world in this field and that other nations are just too slow and cowardly, but that soon they will follow us when we have this new force.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
In spite of all this the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra says the bill has nothing to do with the composition of the forces. I am sure he must have taken a very active, personal dislike to General Allard, the chief of staff, because the only reason that has been put forward by the minister or anyone on his behalf was a remark made by General Allard. He said that he was sure once this bill had been passed and there was no more uncertainty, the forces would settle down and morale would have a chance to improve. This, Mr. Chairman, is the only reason for speed, the only justification given by General Allard, the minister or anyone else as to why this bill should be pressed with what we have always considered to be such unseemly haste. This 
was the reason we could not call more witnesses. The Liberals may have missed their chance. They may have been able to find an ex-service officer with knowledge and freedom to speak who may have upheld the minister's idea.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra says that this bill has nothing to do with morale. Then he says the real effect of it is to give the forces a new and honourable name. Surely, Mr. Chairman, this is highly insulting to those forces that have built up Canada's reputation abroad. This is highly insulting to those serving officers and men who, through two world wars, made it possible for any serviceman wearing a Canadian uniform to walk with pride, no matter in what company he may be. The Royal Canadian Army, the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force have always had a tremendous reputation. However, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra is going to give them a new and honourable name. I wonder, is there any limit to how much abuse the soldiers, sailors and airmen have to take from these members who will go to any lengths in their assertion that, because what they are doing is new, then obviously it must be right. Anyone who gets in the way is an old fuddy-duddy who has done nothing to deserve any consideration, and who is trying to block progress.
I think perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I have dealt sufficiently with the background and the manner in which some of this evidence has been handled by people who should know better. I do not care what party a member represented on that committee or what party he represents in the house, his duty is to weigh carefully the evidence in as objective a manner as possible. His mind should be made up only after a careful and fair consideration of the evidence. The evidence of no witness should be rejected out of hand because it happens to conflict with a preconceived opinion. Due weight and consideration should be given to the person giving evidence, his experience, the position he occupies, his access to information and his ability and willingness to speak freely and frankly to the committee.
I reject any suggestion that any of the witnesses who came before our committee were not trying to give us the truth in so far as they were able.
I have pointed out, and I believe the Minister of Transport has indicated he agrees with me, that serving officers are inhibited in giving their evidence, that they can only give evidence that is in line with the policy they
April 10, 1967

are bound to carry out. This evidence, therefore, cannot be given the same weight as the evidence of independent officers. However, this is not a reflection on their honesty. I believe it is a reflection, perhaps, on this house, as I pointed out some time ago. Certainly, if we are going to call witnesses before a committee, they should be able to give free and honest opinions. I disagreed with the minister when he said that he had the right to indicate what he wanted them to say. Certainly I believe this is a matter which should be looked into by the house.
Be that as it may, the evidence before the committee has been overwhelming, from those who were free to speak, to the effect that unification should not come now. Another group of witnesses said they would not go so far as to say unification would never work, but it certainly would not work now. It certainly needs more study. I hope, Mr. Chairman, to have other opportunities to speak because I firmly believe that many of these officers, after long years of service to the country and with the technical competence they have, should have their opinions put on the record of this house. The next time I speak I hope to be able to quote from their evidence and give a few good examples of their excellent opinions.

Mr. Chairman, a week ago I opened for the opposition, the discussion on Bill No. C-243 and, since that time, we have heard many members from all sides of the house. In fact, looking over the list of speakers, I see that 16 government members, about 20 members of the official opposition, five of the New Democratic Party and three independent members have participated in the discussion and their speeches were fairly extensive; following this, the Social Credit party and the Ralliement Creditiste both participated.

National Defence Act Amendment
In view of the fact that we have also had interventions on a completely separate subject related to defence, the external affairs of the country, it seems to me that we are considering not only the technical aspect of the amendment to the National Defence Act but also the entire program of external affairs of the country.
That is why I found rather strange the words of my hon. friend the member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) when he closed his remarks Friday afternoon by saying:
Therefore, we say, now that everything has been said, let us act, let us vote and the electorate will judge whether this government is right or wrong.
Mr. Chairman, I find this an over-simplification of the problem. True, a blind or a deaf man may, if you will, be forced to vote, and if the electorate has to decide whether the government is right or wrong. I believe that by that time it is a little too late. If we destroy our armed forces by this reorganization, it will then be too late to say: The government has done that.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that ten to 15 years will be required to correct-

It may be that, in this context, I was ahead of the views of the hon. member for, in my first contribution to the debate a week ago, I said that the government had asked or demanded that the house state its views on second reading, and the yea or nay of an hon. member, whether on the government side or in opposition, would not have changed his opinion, as a result of all the testimony we have heard in committee; therefore, the government has proceeded under a false principle, and so there is nothing new there.

April 10, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment
In fact, what we have heard in our ridings is enough to make us realize that people understand the difference between integration and unification. I do not know if the hon. member has underlined that difference, because he left room for doubt in his speech Friday afternoon.
What does the word integration mean? And the word unification? For the information of the hon. member, I feel that the debate-in which the government members took part as much as the opposition members-showed the people what was what. There was a certain amount of reporting, but it is also true that some reporters or newspapermen have become fed up; they cannot make up new headlines, so they get fed up, because they want news, something new. We might organize a dance to create a diversion or change somewhat the present atmosphere.
But, on the other hand, are we not trying to decide a matter of major importance, a fundamental matter, something which we will be unable to get rid of tomorrow? That is tragic for those of us who oppose not only the principle of unification but unification now or later, or unification itself.
I do not accept the principle of unification and I am as sincere in this view as any of those who accept it. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres emphasized many times everybody's good faith and, therefore, blameworthy motives should not be imputed to anybody. On the other hand, I will say this, to him and to all hon. members: the truth always persists and a repetition of good arguments does not weaken them. In certain circumstances, arguments must be repeated, sometimes in one way, sometimes in another way. Therefore, I say that we have not lost our time.
We have heard almost all members of the defence committee. Certainly, a few others will take part in this debate; at least I hope so. I am sure we will hear in a few moments the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Groos), who was chairman of the committee for several weeks. As a former career officer, he should have some observations to make.
Now, I should like to go back to another matter raised by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). I deeply regret that he is not in his seat tonight. He took issue with my colleagues from Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) and Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), as well as myself, charging that we were racists because we objected to certain statements made by General Allard.


Well, I can say he is the one who introduced racialism, as some journalists did, too, who claimed that we were criticizing General Allard because he was a French Canadian, because he spoke French. But why General Allard and not General Moncel, or General Fleury? They too are French Canadians. And also, some criticism has been overlooked-

No, I thought I had indicated clearly that I was through referring to the remarks the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres made last week about General Allard.
As for me, whether the chief of the armed forces is named Smith, Boychuk or Allard, I could not care less. But I maintain that he had no right to speak as he did. After all, our argument was based on a reliable report published in the newspaper La Presse in which he was reported as having condemned the motives of certain members opposed to Bill No. C-243. I shall not repeat his remarks, but I do not think the chief of the armed forces was justified in imputing motives to members of the house. I shall not add anything more, but he had no right to say that.
On a technical matter, it is only natural to disagree, because after all, it is impossible to always reach unanimous agreement.
I feel that even though he disagrees with his former colleagues on that point, they can also be believed. As for him, I am not imputing any motive but, on the other hand, he should not impute any to us either.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I found the intervention by the Minister of Transport the other evening to be rather strange, and this point has been referred to by my colleague from Edmonton-Strathcona and others. It is not so much that he wanted to discuss whether unification was good or bad; he was directing his remarks to something that I think is quite fundamental to a discussion of this bill, and the procedures of this house in arriving at his conclusions on this bill. He was raising a doubt as to whether retired
April 10, 1967

officers should come before a committee to testify on military matters.
The minister said that these officers did not put any evidence before us but that what they said was only a matter of opinion. Gracious me, Mr. Chairman, even before the committee on transport and communications the greater part of the evidence given on the bill that the minister had before the committee was a matter of opinion. If I may say so, there is a great deal of difference between the type of witnesses one would call to speak on a bill such as Bill No. C-243, which deals with military matters, and witnesses who would give evidence on a bill dealing with transport. After all, Mr. Chairman, military men are not out on civvy street; they are specialists and are found only in the armed services. That is where they get their knowledge.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Admittedly some civilians, if one distinguishes them from military persons, are also experts on military theory. I would have hoped that some civilians might have come forward to testify for or against this measure, to give the committee the benefit of their opinions.
It has been suggested that the former officers brought forward to testify were sympathetic to the opposition. I know I put forward the names of several officers on behalf of the official opposition, at the suggestion of my colleagues, but I do not think anyone knew what at least 90 per cent of their testimony would be.

I will not mention names. We did not know what 90 per cent of the testimony was to be. I can say this to the minister, that it was not known what the testimony of the former chief of the defence staff would be. The majority of men who have testified have kept their silence and their counsel. I could have dredged up men by the legion who would damn the minister in no uncertain terms. He should have listened to some telephone calls I received in Edmonton during Easter week from service and ex-service personnel. They spoke about unification. I will
National Defence Act Amendment not repeat what they said about the minister, but they were not complimentary about the legislation he proposes.
Be that as it may, the members of the defence committee needed expert advice about the workings of integration and unification. One cannot say that in the main the retired officers who came before the committee had been retired for many years, or that the minister had discussed or failed to discuss this measure with them. Most of these men had had recent experience, and their testimony must be weighed carefully and must be given grave consideration by all hon. members of the house and by the public.
I know some feel that when a man reaches the rank of major general, rear admiral or air vice marshal that he starts wearing too much gold braid, which gives off some sort of radiation affecting his brain, and that he begins suffering from senility. This is a grave misconception. I suppose, similarly, that editorial writers think this way about publishers. They imagine that "the old man has gone soft in the top story". When it comes to running a newspaper I think that editorial writers, news reporters or cartoonists will agree that the publisher very likely is some streets ahead of the men who criticize him. Of course there are exceptions.
I say to this house that it will be a poor day when we cannot get men to come before a committee to express their views. I will agree that senior serving officials in the department should confine their testimony to facts. As will be seen from the testimony of a number of witnesses, when they were asked questions about confidential matters, about confidential advice they had given to the minister or others, they quite properly claimed privilege. No one insisted that they breach it. It will be to the advantage of the house to adhere to this facet of procedure. Before the Indian affairs and northern development committee the former commissioner of the Northwest Territories had some blunt things to say. When a man of mature judgment and experience who has had a great deal to do with implementing a policy comes forward should we not, as laymen, listen to him? How is one to determine policy? Is one to take only the minister's advice? This is the last thing we ought to do; otherwise we all become rubberstamps for ministerial suggestions.
It will be a happier day when legislative proposals are turned over to committees before second reading, to be accepted or rejected in principle at that stage. The present
April 10, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment measure is a classic example of why our system is not working. The Minister of Finance has said that legislation emanating from the Carter report on taxation will be placed before a committee, as a proposal, before acceptance on second reading. That I think is a step in the right direction. That procedure was followed with the transportation legislation last year, also in the Northwest Territories bill. These are halting steps in the evolution of parliament.

I say this is part of the evolutionary process. What I have suggested ought to be done is in fact done in many legislatures of western Europe. As I say, I think this bill shows, in a classic way, where our procedure has been wrong. This afternoon, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra made a ploy, if one may term it that, saying that we should get on with this bill: "It is so easy, let us get on with it." What is the hurry? I am reminded of a cartoon drawn by Chambers where, standing against the wall, with their hands tied behind their backs, and facing the execution squad are a soldier, a sailor and an airman. In charge of the execution squad are caricatures of the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence. To them is attributed the caption, "We have decided to go on with the execution, but we will postpone the funeral." This is precisely what the government intends to do with the bill. They say, "Pass this bill and we shall defer its implementation.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Vice Admiral Hennessy has said that morale in the navy is high. General Allard in his evidence before the committee said morale would get worse if this bill were not passed. Would morale indeed get worse if this bill is not passed? Remember there is not one member on this side of the house who talks about fighting morale when he talks about morale. As Admiral Landymore said in his testimony in June of last years: Ask me about the morale of men in maritime command; there are two kinds; if you talk about fighting morale there is not one who is not prepared to do his duty and even beyond it; but when it comes to a different kind of morale, job future, certainty, living conditions and all those things, morale is backward. It is in this second sense that we have discussed morale. Never once has there been a question as to the fighting qualities of our forces. Fighting capacity, yes, but that is something which is


related to numbers and training, or the excessive bleed-out of men getting out ahead of time, and a weakness in recruiting brought on by the uncertainty of some of the steps taken toward integration, the "golden bowler" program, for instance, and some of the other things which weakened the direction of the forces.
Now we are faced with this other business of unification. Some may ask: Why repeat these things? As I said to the hon. member for Trois Rivieres, a good argument never loses force by repetition.

The minister is a great one for generalizations. This whole question of integration and unification could have been put forward in a better way. There would have been less uncertainty in the forces; there would have been a greater understanding by the public and by this house if the minister had given us much more information, if he had been fair with hon. members instead of treating us as ignoramuses, as we were treated on a number of occasions. We are not ignoramuses. I do not know what the minister used to think when he was in opposition. Was he then an expert?
The dilemma in which this house finds itself is still unresolved. It is one which has been adverted to by my hon. friend from Edmon-ton-Strathcona, by the hon. member for Greenwood, by the hon. member for Vancouver East and others. It was introduced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he intervened in the debate. It is something to which I myself have adverted during earlier debates with regard to Bill C-243, namely that the objectives of our defence policy have been modified or are to be modified, because the way in which reorganization of our forces is now taking place would make those forces incompatible with the full discharge of the present commitments and objectives of our defence policy.
Defence policy cannot be determined by the nature of our armed forces. That is putting the cart before the horse. Yet, as was pointed out by a number of the witnesses before the committee, we are committing ourselves in this bill to organize our forces in such a way
April 10, 1967

as to lose our ability to fulfil our obligations as we have undertaken them.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs told us clearly the other afternoon that no change in policy had taken place and that none was contemplated for the time being, though perhaps in the future the situation could alter. If that is the case, a much larger question mark has been placed over this bill. This bill is not necessary in order that integration of command may be brought about. There is a great deal of work still to be done. The whole of materiel command has to be organized and brought into operation. The machinery has to go on stream, and it is a long way from that at present. The same applies to training command. There are a number of ancillary and related problems which so far have not even been discovered.
The minister strikes me as an architect, or an engineer who hires a contractor to put up a building of revolutionary design. He puts in the foundations, builds the walls and the roof, closes in the windows, and then says: We had better test the foundations. This is where he has gone wrong.
This bill is completely and utterly unnecessary. In fact, the bringing forward of this idea at the minister's insistence has meant the loss of his most senior advisers and many more whose services we can ill afford to lose. Why? They are all out of step and he is the only one who is in step. As a result of this unresolved question between foreign policy and defence policy I wish to reiterate an argument which has been made earlier today-that the Prime Minister himself must now come into the picture. It is his responsibility as the senior minister to enter this debate and lay out clearly the relationship between the foreign policy of this government and its defence policy in the light of what it proposes to do. Until this is done the basic question behind this proposal will be left unresolved.
