I think it is not without significance that the discussion on this important and far reaching measure is taking place at a time which coincides with the 50th anniversary of the battle of Vimy Ridge, an anniversary which we have officially marked in Canada by sending a contingent of veterans overseas to take part in ceremonies on the site of that battle.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I am ill-equipped to pay adequate tribute to the heroism of those who fought in that battle or in the other battles of that war, or of the second world war, the Korean war, or any of the battles in which Canadian forces have

National Defence Act Amendment taken part. Suffice it to say, however, that this is an area, the area of military accomplishment and of honour on the field of battle, in which Canada has established no mean tradition. Canadians have a very fine tradition of accomplishment militarily on land, on the sea and in the air and I would suggest therefore to the minister, and to hon. members opposite, especially to the Minister of Transport in the light of the speech he made on Friday last, that it would behoove them to take a second look at any measure which, as this measure does, strikes so directly at the heart and the content and the feeling of Canadians with respect to their military traditions, their service traditions, and the traditions of the splendid units which have served Canada so well in the past.
I am not one of those, and I think there are few of them in this chamber, who are opposed to change where change is demonstrated to be beneficial and where it is clearly proven that the change will produce a better result than the situation which now prevails. But I am indeed opposed to change for the sake of change especially where, as on the evidence we have before us so far, we have the opinions, not of reactionaries but of military moderates, of the people who have had training, who have brought their minds and their thoughts, and their desire to serve the best interests of Canada, to bear upon this problem. They have declared themselves overwhelmingly against the proposition that this bill will do any good, and overwhelmingly in favour of the proposition that the bill, on the contrary, will do great damage to the military effectiveness of Canada's Armed Forces.
What have we in effect by way of background for the consideration we are giving this measure tonight? We have here one minister, the Minister of National Defence, against over 30 senior advisers who, because of their disagreement with the policy, have either been compulsorily retired or have taken early retirement. These are not brass hats in the old and opprobrious sense of the word. They are not Colonel Blimps. They are men in whom Canada has a substantial investment in training and in experience, men from whom Canada should be getting the maximum return now in terms of advice and service and in the shaping of the armed forces in line with the accepted policy, and that is the policy of integration and not the policy of unification.
Well, where are they now? Gone, all gone; and the minister remains in the face of the
April 10. 1967

National Defence Act Amendment weight of evidence, adamant, stubborn, determined like a Hitler to give no extra ground in spite of the advice of his senior advisers-nor an inch. It does not matter if it means sacrificing the best interests of the armed forces of this country-not an inch will he give, because he personally is committed; and his personal position to him means more than what any council of moderation would advise, such as some gesture, some adjustment in view of the overwhelming evidence that has been given before the standing committee on national defence.
The minister now blames the press. "Oh," he says, "the effects of this bill have been misrepresented. The controversy has been misreported and distorted in the press." It is not just the senior military advisers; it is the press of the country, never the minister, never his stubbornness, but always somebody else who is wrong. "Yes," he says, "they distorted the meaning of the statements." But then in his discussion in Toronto recently before a group of young Liberals, having attacked the press he went on to attack Admiral Lan-dymore. Having attacked the press because it reported the facts, then he attacked Admiral Landymore; and after that he said, "I hope the press won't report what I have just said." What a childish attitude. And, Mr. Chairman, he was on television. The minister, with all his avowed modernity, forgets there is a modern means of communication which, unfortunately from his point of view, brings home to the public the absurdity of his position.
That is the background against which we are discussing this measure. But while I think it is important to bear these facts in mind and to assess the importance or the significance of the minister's stubborn position, these are not the most important arguments or reasons that we should bring to bear in forming our judgment of the measure. No, the arguments in principle, the laws of principle remain, and they of course outweigh even the considerations of the evidence to which I have been referring.
I repeat, sir, that on the basis of the evidence, on the basis of the facts, there has been no sufficient justification made out to support the far-reaching and the dangerous proposals that are embodied in this bill. There has been no sufficient justification for the headlong plunge into unification, with all the turmoil, and all the upset, and all the loss of efficiency, and all the loss to the services of the senior advisers that it has involved and will involve in the future.

Search as you will, I defy hon. members opposite, or the minister, to show us where is the justification for this measure. Does it lie in the realm of economy? Are we going to save money by this proposed measure? Certainly not. According to the evidence of the distinguished officer who for seven years was chief military adviser of past governments and of this government, there is to be no economy.
If one looked for an illustration of the absurdity of the argument in favour of economy the demonstration of it is complete and total. One could find it in the recent words of the minister himself. He said there was going to be economies but when taxed with the question of what it meant to have one common uniform, did he say it would result in savings? No, he said that when servicemen were doing their ordinary daily work they will retain their working uniforms, and when attending any traditional ceremonies, in messes or elsewhere, they will retain their traditional uniforms. He said that only when walking out will they have a common uniform. What kind of absurdity is that?
So a common uniform means one extra uniform, and what pride can any one man, or any one unit have in the fact that when he or they walk out, instead of wearing a traditional uniform they have to wear a common uniform? What kind of saving is that? What improvement will it bring to their morale; or is it just extra expenditure on an extra uniform which will add nothing in terms of economy or efficiency?
What about efficiency itself? Is the single rank structure going to add to the efficiency of the fighting prowess of the men in the units and of the service themselves? Can it be denied that if we are to have effective defence forces for an effective defence of Canada-and in spite of the minister's intran-sigency that is still the primary responsibility of any government, to ensure the national security of the country-we have to have forces capable of military effort against attack, capable of striking a blow on the sea against any seaborne invasion or follow-up, capable of military effort on land to contain, and to repel, and to defeat any land forces that may attack us?
I see that the minister has just received another message from on high. I mention this in passing, Mr. Chairman.
To continue, we have to have forces capable of effort in the air, capable of beating down an airborne assault on Canada and of attacking troops on land. We have to have forces

April 10, 1967	COMMONS
capable of military effort in the three spheres. If it is necessary to have forces capable of a military effort in three spheres, what possible increase in effectiveness would there be in having them in one uniform instead of three, or in having a single rank structure instead of three. This has not been demonstrated and of course cannot be. What about the national interest; what about Canada's responsibility for maintaining and protecting the integrity of Canada. I suggest the evidence clearly establishes that if this course of unification is proceeded with it will mean that now, and in the foreseeable and definite future, when it comes to the matter of the defence of Canada, once again we will be dependent upon the United States and will not be able to play even our proportionate part in the defence of the North American continent.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
While no one for a moment would suggest that Canada, by itself, can defend its part of the North American continent, nevertheless it is our responsibility to play our full part in the alliances and defence arrangements. This certainly means we must be prepared to integrate closely our forces in these alliances with the forces of those with whom we are allied in respect of the defence of the North American continent. This means the close co-operation of our forces with those of the United States, and we are fortunate that that country is there. How on earth does the minister suggest that this unified force of which he is speaking will be capable of bringing about a more effective Canadian effort, in respect of the type of Canadian responsibilities we have in this sense, than would three integrated forces each capable of its own distinct but coordinated effort in the three areas in which the defence forces must function, namely on the sea, on land, and in the air?
What about the more effective discharge of our defence commitments? Is it here that the bill can be justified? As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton West and other hon. members, we do not even know what our commitments are. The NORAD arrangement is under review at the present time. Is the minister in a position to tell us what will be the result of that review?
If the minister knows, will he tell us what factors govern the decision we are being asked to make here concerning the kind of forces we should have. The NATO commitment is under review at the present time, but we have had no statement either from the
National Defence Act Amendment Minister of National Defence or from the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the direction these negotiations are taking. We have had no statement concerning an alteration in any of our commitments, any new commitments, or the affirmation of an old commitment which might come out of these reviews.
As a result of this bill, if it passes, we will be giving our forces a narrow capability. They will be capable of only one exercise, the exercise which the minister appears to hold in priority to all others.

The minister's speech is capable of a number of interpretations; but the minister's whole attitude is capable of one interpretation and that is that in his view Canada's prime contribution in the defence field is that of an integrated force capable of being transported anywhere in the world for a brushfire operation. Therefore in that sense our commitments and our capabilities must be tailored to the kind of forces we have. Yet, when we have the situation where our commitments are in fact being reviewed, when NORAD and NATO are under review, what should happen is that we should keep our plans flexible so that our forces are tailored to our commitments, instead of our commitments having to be tailored to the kind of defence force this bill inevitably will force upon us.
There is another and I think more important objection than those to which I have referred. Not only do we fail to find any justification for the measure on the grounds I have mentioned, such as economy, efficiency, national interest, and the discharge of our defence commitments, but the primary objection to the whole headlong precipitous course which the minister asks us to follow is jeopardizing the one sound, sensible policy, and that is the policy of integration.
I cannot understand why the minister, who professes to be a progressive and far-sighted man, would run the risk of jeopardizing the policy of integration. This is more than any of us, military advisors or anyone else who has given much thought to this matter based on
14752	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment experience, can possibly understand. In support of my contention that the bill jeopardizes the policy of integration, I should like to refer to the evidence of Air Marshal Miller as given in the committee on national defence. Air Marshal Miller emphasized that he and all the senior military advisors were committed to and were working hard to implement the policy of integration. He also emphasized that the policy was far from complete, and that the program was far from being implemented. He said there were many unresolved problems of a type which required solution in order to lay a sound basis for the development of integrated forces and an integrated and effective effort. He said that this was being, and would be, jeopardized by rushing into unification.
I should like to refer members of the committee to a portion of the air marshal's evidence in this connection as reported in the Gazette of Saturday, April 8. In discussing the theory of integration he said:
There have been various approaches to working and developing an organization that will control the three services. We have had examples of it in the two world wars, and we have examples of it in many of today's activities. So that, I think, anybody who has been in the military, thinks, and has studied the problem of what we have come to call here in the Canadian scene, in the context here, integration. By that I mean the operating of the three services under a single-what I would call-management. A single defence staff, a single planning organization, and a single budgeting arrangement.
This, of course, is the outline of an effective and co-ordinated defence effort. In the course of his evidence, Air Chief Marshal Miller was asked this question:
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
But was there consultation between the military and civilians, or were you under instructions as chief of staff to bring up plans for unification?
To that question he replied:
To the best of my knowledge and recollection,
I have never had any instruction to bring up a unified plan.
I pause there to point out that Air Chief Marshal Miller was chief of defence staff until as recently as July of last year, and he says he had never had any instructions to bring up a unified plan. He had received no instruction to bring up a plan for unification up to July of last year. This bill was introduced last fall, and we are told now, to paraphrase the minister's words and his stand, that the whole welfare and efficiency of the defence effort of the country depends on getting this bill through. It has been too long delayed, we are told. Yet no instructions were given for the preparation

DEBATES	April 10, 1967
of the first plan for a so-called program of unification as late as July of last year when Air Chief Marshal Miller resigned.
Air Chief Marshal Miller gave another answer that I think is of special significance. He was asked whether he would comment on the bill and its dedication to the principle of unification, and said:
Specifically on the bill, I am not familiar with it because I have not had an opportunity to really look at it.
He went on:
On the principle of integration, my own feelings about it are that it might very well be the end result. I do not think it is timely now.
I do not want to substitute my opinion for that of Air Chief Marshal Miller but I think that passage should read, "On the principle of unification, my own feelings about it are that it might very well be the end result." Then he said:
I do not think it is timely now. I have felt that the problem of integration and getting the organization, if you like, was the area where the biggest return in manpower savings and in effective control of military lay, and it was important to get that right before we had ventured into the area of unification.
In those passages and others from the evidence of Air Chief Marshal Miller it becomes quite evident that what concerned the chief military advisers of the government was that they were all committed to the program of integration but felt that that program, and indeed the welfare and effectiveness of Canada's defence forces were jeopardized by the rush into unification. What they were saying was, "Let us get on with and complete the program of integration." Incidentally, that policy and program started long before the present minister was even in the house. It was started shortly after the end of world war II. It was started by the very men whom the minister has been attempting to brand as brass hats and reactionaries. It was started by the military moderates who thought and planned and succeeded in bringing forward plans, modifications and reforms that were in the interests of the country, and it was furthered by a number of ministers before this minister ever came into the house.

I suggest that it is incumbent upon this committee, having assessed the situation, having heard the weight of the evidence, bearing in mind the advice that has been received by the government, and now by the house and the country, from these experts in the field, not to jeopardize the sensible reform of Canada's armed forces and Canada's defence effort. This is a reform which would have the result of a co-ordinated staff,
National Defence Act Amendment co-ordinated planning, integrated supply services and integrated efforts on the part of three fighting services of top efficiency. Those integrated plans should not be jeopardized. Rather, we should say it is not necessary to proceed with this measure now. This is the overwhelming advice we have received. We should say: Let us complete and consolidate the measure of integration. Let us build the integrated forces. Let us build in Canada the most skilful and effective integrated defence forces in the history of any country. But let us not jeopardize all this by succumbing to the dictates of one minister, which have already resulted in the largest purge in the peacetime history of any western country of skilled, seasoned, thoughtful and intelligent military advisers.
Let us get on with the job of building the integrated forces. Let us get on with the job of building the kind of forces which, when it is necessary-and let us pray God it never will be-to call upon them, will repeat, with the same morale, the same splendid tradition, feats such as those to which we have just paid tribute, the feats of Vimy Ridge. Let us get on with the job of building these integrated forces. If we do that with half the skill with which we built the separate forces, and if we can build the kind of Canadian defence forces which will attract Canadians into service and in which they will serve with the same zeal as did the veterans at Vimy, Ortona and at Korea, preserving the traditions and morale of the fighting services, giving them the best backing in integrated command, planning and supply of the best weapons, we can be proud of the job we are doing.
Parliament will have performed a really tremendous service to the country by insisting that this bill be brought to a halt and demanding that the minister and his staff get on with the job of integration, in order that Canada's role in the field of defence may remain sufficiently flexible, so that when our commitments are determined we will have forces of the kind that can be designed to discharge those commitments with the same splendid tradition of heroism, valour and effectiveness as has always characterized Canada's armed forces in her past glorious history.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few comments which I should like to add to this debate. First, there is an evident desire to proceed to a clause by
April 10, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment clause study of the bill, and some demonstrations of impatience that the opposition is taking time to explain its position and bring out the points which it feels should be made for the benefit of Canadians generally, to help them to reach an understanding of what is involved in this so-called unification program. The opposition has a job to do, and its job is to make the objections to this proposed legislation perfectly clear to the Canadian public. Because this is a matter of great importance, the clarification to the public of the matters involved is so important that the necessary time should be taken, and I hope that the impatience of which we saw signs will be less evident in the future than it has in the past.
The rules of parliament are made so that the opposition can bring forward objection to any legislation which is offered by the government, and the time is provided under the rules for this to be done. If the government is not satisfied with the way this has been done, it has a remedy which it can apply.
One reporter wrote that this debate has gone on for 119 days, since the introduction of the white paper in 1964. I am not prepared to vouch for the correctness of that statement, but we do know that the debate has gone on for a long time, and rightly so. Surely the length of the debate and the efforts of the opposition to make good its points against this legislation should be a warning to the government to listen to the opposition and to modify its legislation. What the opposition is asking for, and all it is asking for, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Kamloops, is that this rush to do away with the three branches of our armed forces, the army, the navy and the air force, and to unite them into one single force should be stopped at this stage, until the integration which has been taking place up to date can be thoroughly tried out, and improved upon where necessary. Following this, if it becomes evident that unification, or the abolition of our army, navy and air force and their union into one organization with a single command, a common uniform and a common rank structure, should be carried out, this should not be done until the present state of integration has been thoroughly proven.
The people of Canada have been very uncertain as to what is involved. In listening to the debate over the years the government itself seems to have been very uncertain as to what is involved. It was not until quite recently that the ultimate objective of doing away

with the army, the navy and the air force and uniting them into one body was made clear and that the objections to the whole program became very pronounced. I suggest that the management of this legislation has been mishandled. Uncertainty has been allowed to persist and the government has failed to make its position clear.
I should like to refer the committee to an editorial which appeared in The Legionary, the official organ of the Royal Canadian Legion, for the month of November, 1966. The Legion, through its president, wrote a letter to the Prime Minister. I believe that part of it should be put on the record at this time. It reads as follows:
We have been deeply concerned at some of the public statements which have been made lately, both by those opposing and those proposing complete unification of the Canadian forces. In spite of our best efforts to understand the situation we are compelled to say that, because of the lack of authoritative, clear-cut information and explanation we find ourselves unable at this moment to form a sound judgment on the whole question.
The Royal Canadian Legion is not interested in the partisan politics which appear to be developing in connection with this question. We are, however, deeply concerned about the question of the state and condition of our defence forces at any given time. It appears to us that sufficient thought and planning have not been given to the important questions of tradition, morale and esprit de corps or, if so, the members of Canada's forces and the public have certainly been kept in ignorance.
The point I am trying to make here is that there has been continuous uncertainty, even on the part of the best informed people in this country, concerning the question of the unification of our armed forces. For that reason the government should listen to the opposition and should be prepared to stop the integration process in its present state and to give it a thorough try before proceeding further. That is all that the opposition is asking.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will not take me very long to lay my complaint before the minister. The riding which I represent has always been very interested in navy, army and air cadets. I hope the minister is taking in all of this.
There has always been a great interest in flying in our district. We have an unusually large number of men and women who have their private licence to fly planes. Even the little village some miles from where I live, with a total population of only 1,000, has a small airfield. I believe there are about ten young people in that district who have their private licence for flying planes. There has been a great deal of interest in the district in recent years in respect of the R.C.A.F. Golden Centennials. The people have discussed this group and are anxious to see a full show at Castlegar. I have had letters from practically every municipality in the riding of Kootenay West urging that the Department of National Defence, if it is possible, provide a full air show at Castlegar when this squadron is visiting the interior of British Columbia.
It is for that reason I asked the following question as reported on page 14422 of Hansard for April 3:
I dislike very much intruding twice during one question period-
This is quite correct, Mr. Speaker.
-but this is a matter of urgency.
It is from the point of view of the people I have the honour to represent.
In view of the request by the municipalities In Kootenay West, representing the wishes of the people, that the R.C.A.F. Golden Centennials put on a full show while in Castlegar on July 14,
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and in view of the fact that the Castlegar squadron of the Royal Canadian Air Cadets, Kootenay West, has been chosen as the top squadron in Canada, will favourable consideration be given to the request of the municipalities and the 25,000 spectators expected to attend-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the fourth or fifth time I beg the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) to give us his assistance so that a night train may run between Montreal and Quebec city, at least for the duration of Expo.
I want to explain right away that I do not blame the minister who until now has been extremely kind in offering his help, but to try
14756	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion to get as much assistance as possible to urge the Canadian Pacific authorities to run such a night train. Until now, the only answer we got was in the negative.
Mr. Speaker, here is the whole matter in a nutshell.
Between Montreal and Quebec city, and especially in my immediate area, there are
350,000	people who are poorly served by the Canadian Pacific and who, at Expo time namely, will not be able to leave for Montreal in the morning and come back at night, which means that they will have just a few hours in the afternoon to enjoy Expo.
That night train was requested by the government of my province, through a unanimous motion. It has been requested by about 40 municipalities, by a great number of federal members, of my colleagues here; the project has also been supported by Expo's commissioner general and several special interest groups which have sent resolutions in due form.
In spite of all that, not only does the Canadian Pacific refuse to run the train in question but they even refuse to grant us an interview so that we may state our case.
Mr. Speaker, I charge the Canadian Pacific with gross negligence in its duty towards the people. I should like to remind the management of the Canadian Pacific that they became wealthy through the gifts and grants of the Canadian people, and that they have a moral obligation to the Canadian people to supply them with services that I call essential services. They have no right to treat such important and unanimous requests as this one with the haughtiness they have shown.
I charge the Canadian Pacific with refusing Expo assistance which would be of infinitely greater value than the building they put up, that of guaranteeing reasonable services for all those who wish to visit Expo.
Mr. Speaker, it is not only the people in my area who need this night train; there are thousands of passengers who will not be able to stay in Montreal during Expo and who will have to spend the night in municipalities 50 or 80 miles away from Montreal, when they would like to visit other municipalities after spending the day at Expo.
There are also people in my area who will not be able to reach Montreal by car because of inadequate roads and parking facilities.

the federal parliament and of municipal councils will go and stand on their doorsteps as long as they do not show up to hear us, and this precisely for the purpose of coming to a solution before it is too late, because Expo is opening on April 28.

DIVORCE-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE RELIEF IN CASES OF PROLONGED DESERTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I received a letter from a young woman with five children who had been deserted for over five years, asking about the prospects for changes in the divorce law. I think my experience in receiving this 23033-933
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion letter is no different from the experience of most other hon. members in this chamber.
However, that is not why I raised this question earlier this afternoon. I thought about it for approximately a week because it seemed to me it would take some time for the joint committee to bring in its recommendations to this chamber and to the other place; and then, of course, the government would need time in which to study the recommendations. There are good and sufficient reasons in my opinion for establishing wilful desertion of three years or more as an immediate ground for divorce, and I should like to present these reasons to the Minister of Justice. Before I do so may I compliment him, as many other members have done and will do, on his appointment to that position. We have great faith in him and great hopes for the work he will carry out.
I shall set out some of the reasons for my thinking we should pass a divorce measure without waiting for a full bill, which in my opinion could not come before this house until much later this year, either in October or in November. First there is the burden on the courts. There are some 60,000 people in Canada who have been deserted by their spouses, and since our divorce rate is about
8,000	a year one can see that a considerable burden will be thrown on the courts by applications in connection with this class of case alone.
My second point is that courts have to establish rules with regard to cases of desertion. In many of these cases one of the parties has either bolted from the province or established himself, or herself, a long way from his or her home. This will mean the establishment of special rules which I do not think will need to be established in connection with most of the other classes of application now being considered by the divorce committee, with the possible exception of cases involving people suffering from incurable insanity. The courts need time in which to establish rules, and this alone would eat up several precious months.
In the third place, my mail would indicate that the class of deserted people is the largest single class-with the possible exception of cases involving cruelty-which will have to be considered under the new divorce law. To my mind, when a marriage has broken up for three years or more it is up to this parliament to provide some relief for those who are left behind with the children.
Finally there is this question of the children. The Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and others have indicated that in
14758	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion our new divorce law we must of course consider the needs of the children. This will probably be the most difficult part of drawing up the new divorce law and one which will give the joint committee the greatest concern. But the fact is that after desertion has occurred for three or more years it is probable that any legal remedies which exist will either have been attempted and have worked, or will have been attempted and have failed. So I do not think this particular aspect of divorce reform is a stumbling block in this class of case.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
May I suggest to the minister that he admit limited judicial separation or divorce on that ground, judicial separation being favoured by the Catholic Council and by some of the Protestant faiths. I think we have to pay heed to religious thinking when we bring in our divorce reform. Second, may I suggest to him that this is best done by talking with the house leaders. If we are to have immediate reform in this one specific field it can only come if the members of this place exercise discipline, recognize a need, and say the measure will pass with very short debate. If that is not possible, Mr. Speaker, then that class will have to wait until the fall months come around. But if the minister, through the house leaders, is able to achieve an agreement on this class of case, which to my mind is the most worthy of immediate relief in the process of divorce reform, then perhaps we could have an interim measure presented and passed in a remarkably short time, even though we are in the dying hours of the session. In short, we could have a sort of special centennial project of which we can all be proud and then, later in the fall, take the more leisurely and long-term approach to some very difficult problems in the divorce field.

maintopic: DIVORCE-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE RELIEF IN CASES OF PROLONGED DESERTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) for his kind congratulations and assure him he has introduced a
DEBATES	April 10, 1967
subject with which I will be very much concerned in the months to come. I want to assure him that this is a matter which I and my colleagues regard as being of major importance, one which will get very serious consideration when all the facts are before us.
I think the arguments brought forward by the hon. member are well thought out and reasoned, and I will say quite frankly that they do merit consideration. However, the problem he is really raising is whether this type of legislation is better attacked piecemeal or when introduced as a whole, and whether the spirit of reform and the spirit of the law can be better preserved in one way or in another.
As the hon. member knows, for some time a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons has had the whole question of divorce, including the grounds for relief and the adequacy or otherwise of existing legislation, under serious study. It is expected that this committee will be in a position to report in the not too distant future, and I submit that it might be unfair to the members of this committee, representing as it does both houses of parliament, to introduce any measure of an interim nature which might imply government approval or disapproval of any recommendation which the committee may feel disposed to make.
It is essential that in considering the reform of Canada's divorce law the government should, in the interests of all concerned, view the problem in the broadest possible perspective. The needs of those who are suffering real hardship must of course be taken into account, but it is doubtful whether piecemeal solutions should be envisaged at a time when there is a serious attempt being made to solve the problem as a whole. This is a complex and sensitive problem, and one which must be approached in a spirit of mature deliberation if legislation in keeping with present day realities is to be achieved.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
